class/Team.d:
The Team class represents a faction in a Roblox place. The only valid parent for a Team is in the Teams service. Teams offer a range of features that are useful to developers that can be divided into two rough groups:

  • Features that work 'out of the box'
  • Features developers can program into their game.

Built-in Team Behavior

The following functionality of Teams exists by default and does not require the developer to program any custom behavior.

  • When part of a Team, the name above a player's character Model will be colored to the Team.TeamColor
  • Changing Player.TeamColor will cause Player.Team to switch to the Team with the corresponding Team.TeamColor
  • When using the default player list users will be grouped and displayed together as a team
  • Setting Player.Neutral to true will cause the Player to be disassociated with the team, but it will not change Player.Team or Player.TeamColor
  • When a Player joins a game, they will be allocated to the team with Team.AutoAssignable set to true that has the fewest players. If no auto assignable team is available, Player.Neutral will be set to true
  • When SpawnLocation.Neutral is set to false, only players whose Player.TeamColor matches SpawnLocation.TeamColor can spawn on that SpawnLocation
  • When SpawnLocation.AllowTeamChangeOnTouch is set to true, a player's Player.TeamColor will change to SpawnLocation.TeamColor when their character touches the SpawnLocation

Optional Extended Team Behaviors

Many developers chose to add the following features to teams in their own code.

  • Implement checks in weapon code to prevent friendly fire.
  • Implement checks in doors or other features that allow only certain teams to use them
  • Periodically reassign teams to maintain team balance

This property sets the color of the Team. Determines the Player.TeamColor property of players who are a member of the team.

A lot of Roblox's default team functionality is based on the team color, rather than the name or object. For example, SpawnLocations can be assigned to a team via SpawnLocation.TeamColor. For this reason it is recommended that developers ensure each Team has a unique TeamColor.

Any player which is a part of a team will have their name color changed to the team's TeamColor property. They will also be put underneath the team heading on the player list.

kid.example: team.TeamColor = BrickColor.new("Lapis")

Team.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)

kid.simple: Fires when a player leaves this team: they switched teams, became neutral, or left the game.

A Team is a group players can belong to, like Red Team or Blue Team. Each Team has a color. Players on a team get their name shown in that color and are grouped together in the player list. Team objects must live inside the Teams service.
kid.analogy: A Team is like a jersey color in a school sports day. Everyone wearing red is on the Red Team, sits together on the scoreboard, and starts at the red starting line (red SpawnLocations).
whenToUse: Split players into sides for a game (cops vs robbers, red vs blue).
Count or loop over everyone on one side (GetPlayers).
Make team-only spawn points or team-only doors.
kid.where: Inside the Teams service. Add them in Studio (hover Teams, click +, insert Team) or with `Instance.new("Team")` parented to `game:GetService("Teams")`. Players join a team by setting `player.Team`.

terms.TeamColor: The BrickColor that identifies a team. Many team features match things by this color, so give every team a different one.
terms.BrickColor: One of Roblox's named colors, like "Bright red" or "Lapis".
terms.auto-assign: Roblox putting a joining player on a team by itself, choosing the team with the fewest players.
terms.SpawnLocation: A pad where players appear. It can be locked to one team's color.

examples.title: Create two teams and balance players yourself
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local Teams = game:GetService("Teams")

local function makeTeam(name, colorName)
    local team = Instance.new("Team")
    team.Name = name
    team.TeamColor = BrickColor.new(colorName)
    team.AutoAssignable = false -- we'll choose teams ourselves
    team.Parent = Teams
    return team
end

local red = makeTeam("Red Team", "Bright red")
local blue = makeTeam("Blue Team", "Bright blue")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    -- Put the new player on whichever team has fewer people
    if #red:GetPlayers() <= #blue:GetPlayers() then
        player.Team = red
    else
        player.Team = blue
    end
end)

red.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    print(player.Name .. " joined the Red Team")
end)
explain: Each Team gets a name and a unique TeamColor, and is parented to the Teams service.
AutoAssignable = false stops Roblox from choosing teams for us.
GetPlayers() gives the list of a team's players; # counts them.
Setting player.Team moves the player onto that team, which fires the team's PlayerAdded event.

gotchas: Teams only work when they're directly inside the Teams service.
Give every team a different TeamColor. Spawns and Player.TeamColor match teams by color.
AutoAssignable only evens out teams when players join, not when they leave.
Teams don't block friendly fire on their own. Check teams in your weapon scripts.

examples.title: Print every team and how many players are on it
examples.code:
local Teams = game:GetService("Teams")

while true do
    task.wait(10) -- every 10 seconds
    for _, team in Teams:GetTeams() do
        print(team.Name .. ": " .. #team:GetPlayers() .. " players")
    end
end

For more information on how to teleport players between servers, see Teleporting Between Places.

r.s: The teleport data previously stored by TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData(), or nil if no data was set.

m.d:
This is a setter function for data to be passed to the destination place. On the destination place, this data can be retrieved using Player:GetJoinData() or TeleportService:GetLocalPlayerTeleportData().

For example, the following snippet would send the DataModel.PlaceId and DataModel.JobId in a dictionary passing the teleport data in a TeleportOptions instance using TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData():

-- Server
local teleportOptions = Instance.new("TeleportOptions")
local teleportData = {
    placeId = game.PlaceId,
    jobId = game.JobId
}
teleportOptions:SetTeleportData(teleportData)
TeleportService:TeleportAsync(game.PlaceId, {player}, teleportOptions)

This data could then be retrieved upon arrival using the GetLocalPlayerTeleportData() function as follows:

-- Client
local TeleportService = game:GetService("TeleportService")

local teleportData = TeleportService:GetLocalPlayerTeleportData()
if teleportData then
    local placeId = teleportData.placeId
    local jobId = teleportData.JobId
end

If no teleportData was set in the teleportation function this GetLocalPlayerTeleportData() will return nil.

Allowed data types

Teleport data may only contain value types. It cannot contain Instances or other types that reference engine state, as these cannot safely cross the boundary between servers.

Allowed:

  • Primitives: bool, number, and string
  • Value types such as Vector3, CFrame, Color3, UDim2, NumberSequence, ColorSequence, Enum items, and similar
  • Tables and arrays (without mixed keys) containing only the allowed types above, nested up to a reasonable depth and size

Not allowed (these will be removed from the data before the teleport completes):

  • Instance and instance references
  • Connections, RBXScriptSignal, and functions
  • SharedTable
  • Types that reference engine or DataModel state, such as InputObject, RaycastParams, and RaycastResult

If teleport data contains a disallowed type, that value is removed and an error is written to the developer console. Convert instance references to plain values (for example, a numeric ID or a string path).

For more information on how to send and receive user data along with teleports, see, see Teleporting Between Places.
m.s: Setter function for data to be passed to the destination place.

p.s: Data to be passed to the destination place.

m.d:
This function returns the PlaceId and JobId of the server the user with the given UserId is in, provided it is in the same game as the current place.

Then, TeleportService:TeleportToPlaceInstance() can be called with this information to allow a user to join the target user's server.

Upon a successful lookup, the function returns the following values:

# Name Type Description
1 currentInstance bool A bool indicating if the user was found in the current instance
2 error string An error message in the event of the lookup failing
3 placeId int64 The PlaceId of the server the user is in
4 instanceId string The JobId of the server the user is in

If there is a problem during lookup, such as the user being offline, an error is thrown. It is recommended that you wrap calls to this function in pcall.

Limitations

You should be aware of the following limitations when using this function:

  • This function can only be called by the server.
  • This function may fail to return the correct information if the user is teleporting.
  • It is possible for this function to throw an error, hence developers should wrap it in a LuaGlobals.pcall() (see example below)
  • As this function returns the JobId of the server and not the access code returned by TeleportService:ReserveServerAsync(), the ID returned is not appropriate for use with reserved servers.

Studio Limitation

Note that this service does not work during playtesting in Roblox Studio; to test aspects of your experience using it, you must publish the experience and play it in the Roblox application.

m.d:
This function retrieves a teleport setting saved using TeleportService:SetTeleportSetting() using the given key.

This method is intended for use on the client only and should not be used on the server.

Teleport settings are preserved across teleportations within the same game. This means data can be saved using TeleportService:SetTeleportSetting() in one place and retrieved using GetTeleportSetting in another place the user has been teleported to.

For example, in a game that allowed crouching you could save whether the user is currently crouching prior to teleporting as a teleport setting. This could then be retrieved in the destination place after the teleportation:

local TeleportService = game:GetService("TeleportService")

local isCrouching = TeleportService:GetTeleportSetting("isCrouching")

If no teleport setting exists under the given key, this function will return nil.

Differences from GlobalDataStores

Although they share some similarities, there are some key differences between teleport settings and datastores:

  • GlobalDataStore:SetAsync() stores the data on Roblox servers whereas SetTeleportSetting stores the data locally
  • Data stored in a GlobalDataStore is preserved after the user leaves the game universe whereas teleport settings are not
  • GlobalDataStores can only be accessed on the server, whereas teleport settings can only be accessed on the client
  • GlobalDataStores have usage limits, whereas teleport settings do not

In general teleport settings should be used to preserve client side information within a single play session across different places in a game. GlobalDataStores should be used to save important player data that needs to be accessed across player sessions.

Teleport settings and security

As teleport settings are stored locally, it is possible they can be manipulated by malicious users. This risk can be mitigated by employing server side validation.

Studio Limitation

Note that this service does not work during playtesting in Roblox Studio; to test aspects of your experience using it, you must publish the experience and play it in the Roblox application.
m.s: Retrieves a teleport setting saved using `Class.TeleportService:SetTeleportSetting()` using the given key.

p.s: The key the value was stored under using TeleportService:SetTeleportSetting().

r.s: The value stored under the given key.

m.d:
This function returns an access code that can be used to teleport players to a reserved server, along with the server's DataModel.PrivateServerId. It can only be called on the server.

Reserved Servers

You can access reserved servers using:

  • TeleportService:TeleportAsync() with the TeleportOptions.ReservedServerAccessCode parameter.
  • TeleportService:TeleportToPrivateServer(), with the access code ReserveServerAsync returns.
  • A server is started when the access code is first used.
  • Access codes remain valid indefinitely, meaning reserved servers can still be joined if no game server is running (in this case a new server will be started).

You can see if the current server is a reserved server by using the following code:

local isReserved = game.PrivateServerId ~= "" and game.PrivateServerOwnerId == 0

The DataModel.PrivateServerId is constant across all server instances associated with the server access code, the DataModel.JobId is not.

Studio Limitation

Note that this service does not work during playtesting in Roblox Studio; to test aspects of your experience using it, you must publish the experience and play it in the Roblox application.

Cross-Platform Play

Players on Xbox and PlayStation with cross‑play disabled will arrive in a different server than players with cross‑play enabled. This can cause multiple game servers with the same PrivateServerId to exist. You can use DataModel.MatchmakingType to differentiate these game servers.

This function sets the custom teleport GUI that will be shown to the local user during teleportation, prior to the teleport being invoked.

Note, the teleport GUI will not be used if the destination place is in a different game. It will also not persist across multiple teleports and will need to be set prior to each one.

This function should only be used on the client. If the teleportation function is called from the server (as is the case with TeleportService:TeleportAsync()) then this function should be called on the client prior to this. One way of doing this is listening to a RemoteEvent that fires several seconds before teleportation.

Loading screen

During a teleport, while the destination place is loading, the customLoadingScreen is parented to the CoreGui. Once the place has loaded the loading screen is parented to nil.

This ScreenGui can be fetched at the destination place using TeleportService:GetArrivingTeleportGui(), allowing you to parent it to the PlayerGui and perform your own transitions.

You are advised to also parent the ScreenGui to the PlayerGui in the start place while the teleport is initiating.

External references

The teleport GUI and all of its descendants are carried to the destination place, but any property that references an Instance outside the GUI's own tree is cleared during the teleport. For example, a Sound inside the GUI whose SoundGroup points to a SoundGroup under SoundService will arrive with that reference set to nil, because the target lives outside the GUI and cannot safely cross the boundary between servers.

References that point to other instances within the GUI tree are preserved. If your loading screen depends on an external instance, recreate that instance inside the GUI tree.

Studio Limitation

Note that this service does not work during playtesting in Roblox Studio; to test aspects of your experience using it, you must publish the experience and play it in the Roblox application.

m.d:
This function stores a value under a given key that persists across all teleportations in the same game.

This method is intended for use on the client only and should not be used on the server.

The stored value can later be retrieved using TeleportService:GetTeleportSetting(). This will work in the current place and any subsequent places the Players.LocalPlayer teleports to, provided they are in the same game.

For example, in a game that allowed crouching you could save whether the user is currently crouching prior to teleporting as a teleport setting:

local TeleportService = game:GetService("TeleportService")

local isCrouching = false
TeleportService:SetTeleportSetting("isCrouching", isCrouching)

The stored value may only contain value types. It cannot contain Instances or other types that reference engine state, as these cannot safely cross the boundary between servers.

Allowed values:

  • Primitives: a bool, a number, or a string
  • Value types such as Vector3, CFrame, Color3, UDim2, NumberSequence, ColorSequence, Enum items, and similar
  • A table without mixed keys (all strings or all integers) containing only the allowed types above

Not allowed (these will be removed before the teleport completes):

  • Instance and instance references
  • Connections, RBXScriptSignal, and functions
  • SharedTable
  • Types that reference engine or DataModel state, such as InputObject, RaycastParams, and RaycastResult

If a stored setting contains a disallowed type, that value is removed and an error is written to the developer console. Convert instance references to plain values (for example, a numeric ID or a string path).

If data is already stored under the given key, the previous value will be overwritten by the new value.

Differences from GlobalDataStores

Although they share some similarities, there are some key differences between teleport settings and datastores:

  • GlobalDataStore:SetAsync() stores the data on Roblox servers whereas SetTeleportSetting stores the data locally
  • Data stored in a GlobalDataStore is preserved after the user leaves the game universe whereas teleport settings are not
  • GlobalDataStores can only be accessed on the server, whereas teleport settings can only be accessed on the client
  • GlobalDataStores have usage limits, whereas teleport settings do not

In general teleport settings should be used to preserve client side information within a single play session across different places in a game. GlobalDataStores should be used to save important player data that needs to be accessed across player sessions.

Teleport settings and security

As teleport settings are stored locally, it is possible they can be manipulated by malicious users. This risk can be mitigated by employing server side validation.

m.d:
This function serves as the all-encompassing method to teleport a player or group of players from one server to another. It can be used to:

  • Teleport players to a different place.
  • Teleport players to a specific server.
  • Teleport players to a reserved server.

Server-Only

This method can only be called from the server. If you need to initiate a teleport from the client, use a RemoteEvent to signal the server, then call TeleportService:TeleportAsync() from a server Script. Client-side teleports using TeleportService:Teleport() is not recommended for new work. See Teleport between places for more information.

Group Teleport Limitations

  • Groups of players can only be teleported within a single experience.
  • No more than 50 players can be teleported with a single TeleportService:TeleportAsync() call.

Potential Errors

This is a list of potential reasons a teleport may fail, ranging from invalid teleports to network issues.

Error Description
Invalid placeId The provided place ID is below 0.
Players empty The provided list of players to teleport is empty.
List of players instances is incorrect Any of the provided players is not a Player object.
TeleportOptions not of correct type The provided teleportOption is not a TeleportOptions object.
TeleportAsync called from Client The client called TeleportAsync, which can only be called from the server.
Incompatible Parameters Conflicting teleport options were used and TeleportService doesn't know where to send the player.

Conflicting TeleportOption parameters:
* ReservedServerAccessCode and ServerInstanceId
* ShouldReserveServer and ServerInstanceId
* ShouldReserveServer and ReservedServerAccessCode

For more information on how to teleport players between servers and receive user data from a teleport, see Teleport between places.

This function fires when the Players.LocalPlayer enters the place following a teleport. The teleportData and customLoadingScreen are provided as arguments.

When fetching teleportData and the customLoadingScreen you are advised to use TeleportService:GetLocalPlayerTeleportData() and TeleportService:GetArrivingTeleportGui() instead. This is because these functions can be called immediately without having to wait for this event to fire.

This event should be connected immediately in a LocalScript parented to ReplicatedFirst. Otherwise, when the connection is made the event may have already fired.

Loading Screen

During a teleport, while the destination place is loading, the customLoadingScreen is parented to the CoreGui. Once the place has loaded the loading screen is parented to nil.

If you wish to preserve the customLoadingScreen and perform your own transitions, you will need to parent it to the local player's PlayerGui. For example, using the following code inside a LocalScript in ReplicatedFirst:

local TeleportService = game:GetService("TeleportService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedFirst = game:GetService("ReplicatedFirst")

TeleportService.LocalPlayerArrivedFromTeleport:Connect(function(customLoadingScreen, teleportData)
    local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
    ReplicatedFirst:RemoveDefaultLoadingScreen()

    customLoadingScreen.Parent = playerGui
    -- animate screen here
    wait(5)
    -- destroy screen
    customLoadingScreen:Destroy()
end)

The customLoadingScreen will not be used if the destination place is in a different game.

Studio Limitation

Note that this service does not work during playtesting in Roblox Studio; to test aspects of your experience using it, you must publish the experience and play it in the Roblox application.

class/Terrain.d:
The Terrain class lets you create dynamically morphable environments. It is based on a 4×4×4 grid of cells, where each cell has a number between 0 and 1 representing how much the geometry should occupy the cell, and the material of the cell. The occupancy determines how the cell will morph together with surrounding cells, and the result is the illusion of having no grid constraint.

For more information, see Terrain.

Metals only reflect light the same color as the metal, and they reflect much more light than non-metals. Most materials in the real world can be categorized either metals or non-metals. m.d:
This property modifies the lighting of the surface by adding bumps, dents, cracks, and curves without adding more polygons.

Normal maps are RGB images that modify the surface's normal vector used for lighting calculations. The R, G, and B channels of the NormalMap correspond to the X, Y, and Z components of the local surface vector respectively, and byte values of 0 and 255 for each channel correspond linearly to normal vector components of -1 and 1.016 respectively. This range is stretched slightly from -1 to 1 so that a byte value of 127 maps to exactly 0. The normal vector's Z axis is always defined as the direction of the underlying mesh's normal. A uniform (127,127,255) image translates to a completely flat normal map where the normal is everywhere perpendicular to the mesh surface. This format is called "tangent space" normal maps. Roblox does not support world space or object space normal maps.

Incorrectly flipped normal components can make bumps appear like indents. If you import a normal map and notice the lighting looks off, you may need to invert the G channel of the image. The X and Y axes of the tangent space frame correspond to the X and Y directions in the image after it's transformed by the mesh UVs. If you view your normal map in an image editor as if it were displayed on a surface, normals pointing towards the right side of the screen should appear more red, and normals pointing towards the top side of your screen should appear more green.

The terms "DirectX format" and "OpenGL format" are sometimes used to describe whether the G channel of the normal map is inverted or not. Roblox expects the OpenGL format.

Roblox expects imported meshes to include tangents. Modeling software may also refer to this as "tangent space" information. If you apply a normal map and it does not seem to make any visual difference, you may need to re-export your mesh along with its tangent information from modeling software.

class/TextBox.d:
A TextBox allows the player to provide text input. It behaves similarly to a TextButton, except that a single TextBox can be put in focus by clicking, tapping, or gamepad selection. While in focus, the player can use a keyboard to change the Text property.

  • If there is no text, the PlaceholderText will be visible. This is useful prompting players of the kind or format of data they should input.
  • By default, the ClearTextOnFocus property is enabled and ensures there is no existing text when a TextBox is focused. This may not be desirable for text that should be editable by the player.
  • The MultiLine property allows players to enter multiple lines of text with newline characters (\n).

Focus State

It is possible to detect and change the focus state of a TextBox:

  • You can use CaptureFocus when a dialogue appears so that the player doesn't have to click on a TextBox when it becomes available; you can use ContextActionService:BindAction() to bind a certain key to focus a TextBox using this function. When a TextBox comes into focus, the Focused event fires.
  • You can detect if a certain TextBox is in focus by using IsFocused. Alternatively, UserInputService:GetFocusedTextBox() can be used to check if any TextBox is in focus.
  • When the player is done inputting text, the FocusLost event fires, indicating if the player pressed Enter to submit text along with the InputObject that caused the loss of focus. When using on-screen keyboards on mobile and console, ReturnPressedFromOnScreenKeyboard may also fire.
  • If some more important matter comes up during gameplay, you can ReleaseFocus of the TextBox so that a player's keyboard input returns to your game.

Text Editing

A TextBox supports text selection through its CursorPosition and SelectionStart properties. Using GetPropertyChangedSignal, you can detect when a selection changes. Additionally, it is possible for players to copy and paste text within a TextBox, enabling basic clipboard support. When the cursor moves outside the visible area while typing or navigating, the TextBox automatically scrolls its viewport to keep the cursor in view.

Text Filtering Notice Games that facilitate player-to-player communication using text, such as custom chat or nametags, must properly filter such text using TextService:FilterStringAsync() or Chat:FilterStringAsync(). If this is not properly done, your game may receive moderation action.

kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.ClearTextOnFocus = false -- keep the text when clicked

m.d:
This property provides a copy of Text that contains exactly what is being rendered by the TextBox. This is useful for eliminating style tags used for rich text markup; for example, when RichText is enabled, the ContentText property shows the text as it appears to the user.

RichText Text ContentText
false <b>Hello,<br/> world!</b> <b>Hello,<br/> world!</b>
true <b>Hello,<br/> world!</b> Hello,
world!
m.s: A copy of `Class.TextBox.Text` that contains exactly what is being rendered by the `Class.TextBox`.

kid.simple: Read-only. The text exactly as players see it. If RichText is on, the formatting tags like are removed. For Text = "Hi" with RichText on, ContentText is "Hi".
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
print(box.ContentText)

m.d:
This property determines the offset of the text cursor in bytes, or -1 if the TextBox is not currently being edited. A value of 1 represents the position before the first byte in the Text property. When used in conjunction with the SelectionStart property, it is possible to both get and set selected text within a TextBox.

Note that the units of this property are bytes and that many unicode characters such as emoji are longer than 1 byte. For instance, if a player types in "Hello👋" ("Hello" immediately followed by the waving hand sign), the cursor position would be 10, not 7, since the emoji uses 4 bytes.
m.s: Determines the offset of the text cursor in bytes, or `-1` if there is no cursor.

kid.simple: Where the typing cursor is, counted in bytes starting at 1 (before the first character). -1 means the player isn't typing in the box. Used with SelectionStart to find selected text.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box:GetPropertyChangedSignal("CursorPosition"):Connect(function()
	print("Cursor at", box.CursorPosition)
end)
kid.gotcha: It counts bytes, not letters. An emoji is 4 bytes, so 'Hello' plus a waving-hand emoji puts the cursor at 10, not 7.

local box = script.Parent
box.Font = Enum.Font.GothamBold

box.MultiLine = true -- good for writing a note or letter

m.d:
Comma-separated list of OpenType feature tags applied when the TextBox shapes and renders its text, such as zero for slashed zeros or ss03 for a stylistic set. Defaults to an empty string (no additional features).

Each entry uses standard OpenType feature-string syntax (for example, zero or ss03). Only a supported subset is applied; an unsupported feature, malformed string, or bracketed partial-enabling syntax (for example, zero[1:3]) is rejected, with the reason in OpenTypeFeaturesError.

Supports styling.
m.s: Applies OpenType typographic features to the text rendered by the `Class.TextBox`.

kid.simple: Turns on special font features using short codes separated by commas, like "zero" for a zero with a slash through it. Empty (default) means none. If a code doesn't work, OpenTypeFeaturesError says why.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.OpenTypeFeatures = "zero" -- slashed zeros, so 0 doesn't look like O

m.d:
Read-only error, if any, from parsing and applying OpenTypeFeatures. Defaults to an empty string when the requested features applied successfully.

An error is produced when:

  • The feature string is malformed and cannot be parsed.
  • A requested feature is not in the supported set.
  • A bracketed range syntax is used (partial feature enabling is not supported).
m.s: Read-only property that describes why the `Class.TextBox.OpenTypeFeatures` string could not be applied.

kid.simple: Read-only. Empty when OpenTypeFeatures worked. Otherwise a message like "Unsupported feature: xyz" telling you what went wrong.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
if box.OpenTypeFeaturesError ~= "" then
	warn(box.OpenTypeFeaturesError)
end

m.d: Sets the text color that gets used when no text has been entered into the TextBox.
m.s: Sets the text color that gets used when no text has been entered into the `TextBox`.

kid.simple: The color of the hint text (PlaceholderText) shown when the box is empty. Usually a light gray.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.PlaceholderColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(150, 150, 150)

m.d: Sets the text that gets displayed when no text has been entered into the TextBox.
m.s: Sets the text that gets displayed when no text has been entered into the `TextBox`.

kid.simple: Gray hint text shown while the box is empty, like "Type your name...". It disappears when the player types.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.PlaceholderText = "Enter a code..."

m.d:
This property determines whether the TextBox renders the Text string using rich text formatting. Rich text uses simple markup tags to style sections of the string in bold, italics, specific colors, and more.

Note that when the TextBox has this property enabled and the box gains focus, the player will be able to edit and interact with the complete XML string, including all of the formatting tags. When focus is lost, the text will automatically parse and render the tags as rich text.
m.s: Determines whether the `TextBox` renders the `Class.TextBox.Text|Text` string using rich text formatting.

kid.simple: When true, you can style parts of the text with tags like bold, italic or red. While the player is typing, they see the raw tags; the styling shows after they click away.
kid.example: local box = script.Parent box.RichText = true box.Text = "You found a golden sword!"

m.d: Determines the starting position of a text selection, or -1 if the TextBox has no range of selected text. This property uses the same positioning logic as CursorPosition. SelectionStart will be greater than CursorPosition if the cursor is at the beginning of a selection, and less than CursorPosition if the cursor is at the end.
m.s: Determines the starting position of a text selection.

kid.simple: Where the selected (highlighted) text starts, using the same counting as CursorPosition. -1 means nothing is selected.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
if box.SelectionStart ~= -1 then
	print("Player has text selected")
end

m.d: If set to true, input native to the platform is used instead of Roblox's built-in keyboard.
m.s: If set to `true`, input native to the platform is used instead of Roblox's built-in keyboard.

kid.simple: When true, the device's own keyboard (like your phone's normal keyboard) is used instead of Roblox's built-in one.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.ShowNativeInput = true

m.d:
This property determines the text content rendered by the TextBox element. The visual properties of the string rendered to the screen is determined by TextColor3, TextTransparency, TextSize, FontFace, and other properties.

It is possible to render emoji such as 👋 and other symbols. These special symbols aren't affected by the TextColor3 property.

This property may contain newline characters, but it is not possible to type newline characters within the Properties window. Similarly, this property may contain a tab character, but it will render as a space instead.
m.s: Determines the string rendered by the `TextBox` element.

kid.simple: The words shown. When the player types, this changes to what they typed. You can use \n in a script to start a new line.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.Text = "Line one\nLine two"

m.d:
This read-only property reflects the absolute size of rendered text in offsets. In other words, if you were to try to fit text into a rectangle, this property would reflect the minimum dimensions of the rectangle you would need in order to fit the text.

Using TextService:GetTextSize(), you can predict what TextBounds will be on a TextLabel given a string, Font, TextSize and frame size.
m.s: The size of a `TextBox` element's text in offsets.

kid.simple: Read-only. The size in pixels of the box the text actually needs. Handy for making a background exactly fit the text.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
print("Text needs", box.TextBounds.X, "by", box.TextBounds.Y, "pixels")

m.dep: This item has been superseded by TextBox.TextColor3 which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use TextColor3 instead.

m.d: This property determines the color of non-placeholder text rendered by the TextBox. Text is rendered after the text stroke.
m.s: Determines the color of non-placeholder rendered text.

kid.simple: The color of the text. (Not the placeholder text; that's PlaceholderColor3.)
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255) -- white text

m.d:
TextDirection in which the TextBox renders its text. Defaults to TextDirection.Auto, which picks direction from the text content so right-to-left scripts render right-to-left. TextDirection.LeftToRight and TextDirection.RightToLeft force left-to-right or right-to-left rendering.

Supports styling.
m.s: Direction in which the text is rendered.

kid.simple: Which way the text reads. Auto (default) figures it out from the language, so languages like Arabic read right-to-left. You can force LeftToRight or RightToLeft.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextDirection = Enum.TextDirection.Auto

m.d: This property determines whether the player can change the Text through input. It is recommended to disable ClearTextOnFocus when this property is disabled, otherwise the text can be cleared on-focus.
m.s: Determines whether the player can change the `Class.TextBox.Text|Text`.

kid.simple: Whether the player can change the text. Set false to make a box people can select and copy from, but not change.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextEditable = false
box.ClearTextOnFocus = false -- otherwise clicking would still wipe it
kid.gotcha: Turn off ClearTextOnFocus too, or clicking will erase the text.

m.d: Whether the text fits within the constraints of the TextBox.
m.s: Whether the text fits within the constraints of the `TextBox`.

kid.simple: Read-only. true if all the text fits inside, false if some of it is cut off.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
if not box.TextFits then
	print("Text is too long for this box!")
end

m.d:
This property determines whether text is scaled so that it fills the box's entire space. When enabled, TextSize is ignored and TextWrapped is automatically enabled. When this property is used for on-screen UI, it may be helpful to use a UITextSizeConstraint to restrict the range of possible text sizes.

See TextLabel.TextScaled for additional recommendations when using this property.
m.s: Changes whether text is resized to fit within the `TextBox`.

kid.simple: When true, the text automatically grows or shrinks to fill the whole box (TextSize is ignored and wrapping turns on). Great for BillboardGuis and SurfaceGuis.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextScaled = true
kid.gotcha: Text can become tiny and hard to read. Add a UITextSizeConstraint to set a min/max size, and don't combine it with AutomaticSize.

m.d: This property determines the height in offsets of one line of rendered text. The unit is in offsets, not points as in many document editing programs.
m.s: Determine the line height of text in offsets.

kid.simple: How tall one line of text is, in pixels. 14 is small, 24 is medium, 48 is big. Ignored when TextScaled is on.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextSize = 24
kid.gotcha: Try not to go below 9; tiny text is hard to read for many players.

m.d: This property sets the color of the stroke (outline) of the rendered text. This property and TextStrokeTransparency determine the visual appearance of the text stroke.
m.s: Determines the color of the text stroke (outline).

kid.simple: The color of the outline drawn around each letter. Only shows when TextStrokeTransparency is less than 1.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextStrokeColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 0) -- black outline
box.TextStrokeTransparency = 0             -- make it visible
kid.gotcha: For thicker or gradient outlines, use a UIStroke instead.

m.d:
This property sets the transparency of the stroke (outline) of the rendered text. This property and TextStrokeColor3 determine the visual appearance of the text stroke.

Since text stroke is simply multiple renderings of the same transparency, this property is essentially multiplicative on itself four times over; for example a TextStrokeTransparency of 0.5 appears about the same as TextTransparency of 0.0625, or 0.5^4.
m.s: Determines the transparency of the text stroke (outline).

kid.simple: How see-through the letter outline is. 1 (default) = no outline, 0 = solid outline. The outline is drawn several times stacked, so even 0.5 looks quite solid; 0.75 to 1 gives a soft outline.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextStrokeTransparency = 0.5

m.d: This property determines the transparency of all the text rendered by the TextBox.
m.s: Determines the transparency of the rendered text.

kid.simple: How see-through the text is. 0 = solid, 1 = invisible. Doesn't affect the background box (that's BackgroundTransparency).
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local box = script.Parent
-- Fade the text out over 1 second
TweenService:Create(box, TweenInfo.new(1), {TextTransparency = 1}):Play()

m.d: Controls the truncation of the text displayed in the TextBox.
m.s: Controls the truncation of the text displayed in the `TextBox`.

kid.simple: What to do with text that's too long to fit. None (default) just cuts it off. AtEnd replaces the end with "...". SplitWord can cut in the middle of a word.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextTruncate = Enum.TextTruncate.AtEnd -- "A really long na..."

m.dep: This item has been superseded by TextBox.TextWrapped which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use TextWrapped instead.

m.d:
When enabled, this property will render text on multiple lines within a TextBox element's space so that TextBounds will never exceed the GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize of the element.

This is achieved by breaking long lines of text into multiple lines. Line breaks will prefer whitespace; should a long unbroken word exceed the width of the element, that word will be broken into multiple lines.

If further line breaks would cause the vertical height of the text (the Y component of TextBox.TextBounds) to exceed the vertical height of the element (the Y component of GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize), then that line will not be rendered at all.
m.s: Determines if text wraps to multiple lines within the `TextBox` element space, truncating excess text.

kid.simple: When true, long text continues on the next line instead of running off the side. It prefers to break at spaces. Lines that don't fit vertically aren't shown.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextWrapped = true

m.d:
This property determines the horizontal alignment of text rendered within the TextBox element's space. It can be used in conjunction with TextYAlignment to fully determine text alignment on both axes.

This property does not affect the read-only properties TextBounds and TextFits.
m.s: Determines the horizontal alignment of the rendered text.

kid.simple: Lines the text up sideways inside the box: Left, Center (default) or Right.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextXAlignment = Enum.TextXAlignment.Left

m.d:
This property determines the vertical alignment of text rendered within the TextBox element's space. It can be used in conjunction with TextXAlignment to fully determine text alignment on both axes.

This property does not affect the read-only properties TextBounds and TextFits.
m.s: Determines the vertical alignment of the rendered text.

kid.simple: Lines the text up up-and-down inside the box: Top, Center (default) or Bottom.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.TextYAlignment = Enum.TextYAlignment.Top

m.d: Forces the client to focus on the TextBox.
m.s: Forces the client to focus on the `TextBox`.

kid.simple: Puts the typing cursor into this box right away, as if the player clicked it. Handy when a chat or code window opens.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box:CaptureFocus() -- player can start typing immediately

m.d: Returns true if the TextBox is focused or false if it is not.
m.s: Whether the TextBox currently has focus.

r.s: Returns true if the TextBox is focused or false if it is not.

kid.simple: Returns true if the player is typing in this box right now, false if not.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
if box:IsFocused() then
	print("Player is typing")
end

m.d: Forces the client to unfocus the TextBox. The submitted parameter lets you override the enterPressed parameter in the TextBox.FocusLost event.
m.s: Forces the client to unfocus the TextBox.

p.s: Whether the TextBox.FocusLost event's enterPressed parameter reports true, as if the player pressed Enter to submit text. Defaults to false.

kid.simple: Takes the typing cursor out of this box, so keyboard keys control the game again. Pass true to make FocusLost report it like Enter was pressed.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box:ReleaseFocus() -- stop typing
-- box:ReleaseFocus(true) -- same, but FocusLost's enterPressed will be true

m.d:
This event fires when the TextBox gains focus, typically when a player clicks/taps on the TextBox to begin text entry. Also fires if TextBox focus is forced through CaptureFocus().

This event can be used alongside FocusLost to track when a TextBox both gains and loses focus.
m.s: Fires when the `TextBox` gains focus.

kid.simple: Fires when the player starts typing in the box (clicks or taps it, or CaptureFocus is called).
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.Focused:Connect(function()
	print("Player started typing")
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the TextBox loses its focus, typically when a player clicks/taps outside of it or presses Enter. Also fires if TextBox focus release is forced through ReleaseFocus().

This event can be used alongside FocusLost to track when a TextBox both gains and loses focus.
m.s: Fires when the `TextBox` loses its focus.

p.s: A boolean indicating whether the client pressed Enter to lose focus (true) or not (false).
An InputObject instance indicating the type of input that caused the TextBox to lose focus.

kid.simple: Fires when the player stops typing in the box, by pressing Enter or clicking somewhere else. It tells you enterPressed (true if they pressed Enter) and the input that caused it. The best place to read what they typed.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.FocusLost:Connect(function(enterPressed, inputThatCausedFocusLoss)
	if enterPressed then
		print("Player submitted:", box.Text)
	end
end)

m.d: On mobile and console, this event fires when the TextBox is focused and the player presses the on-screen keyboard's return/enter button.
m.s: Fires when the `TextBox` is focused and the player presses the on-screen keyboard's return/enter button.

kid.simple: On phones and consoles, fires when the player presses the Return/Enter key on the on-screen keyboard while typing in this box.
kid.example:
local box = script.Parent
box.ReturnPressedFromOnScreenKeyboard:Connect(function()
	print("Done typing on the on-screen keyboard")
end)

kid.simple: A TextBox is a box the player can click and type into. Use it for things like entering a code, naming a pet, or a custom chat. When they finish typing, you read what they wrote from its Text property.
kid.analogy: A TextBox is like a blank line on a form: 'Name: ____'. The player fills it in, and you read what they wrote.
whenToUse: Entering a redeem code
Naming a pet, house or team
A search box in a shop or inventory
Custom chat or message boards
kid.where: Inside a ScreenGui (or a SurfaceGui/BillboardGui in PlayerGui). Read the typed text in a LocalScript, then send it to the server with a RemoteEvent if the server needs it.

terms.UI / GUI: User Interface: the buttons, menus, text and pictures drawn on the screen or on things in the game.
terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. All UI code goes in LocalScripts.
terms.ScreenGui: The invisible container that holds UI shown on the player's screen. It must be inside the player's PlayerGui (put it in StarterGui in Studio).
terms.parent: The object something is placed inside.
terms.UDim2: The value used for Size and Position: (X Scale, X Offset, Y Scale, Y Offset). Scale is a fraction (0 to 1) of the parent's size; Offset is exact pixels.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on the screen.
terms.transparency: How see-through something is. 0 = solid, 1 = invisible.
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green and blue amounts, like Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0) for red.
terms.font: The style of the letters, like Arial, Comic, or a blocky game font.
terms.rich text: Text with simple tags inside it, like word, that make parts bold, italic or colored.
terms.grapheme: One visible character, like a letter, a number, or a symbol.
terms.wrap: When text reaches the edge, it continues on the next line.
terms.truncate: Cut off text that's too long, often adding '...' at the end.
terms.read-only: You can read the value but not change it.
terms.localization: Translating text into the player's language.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something better. Don't use it in new code.
terms.focus: When a TextBox is 'focused', the typing cursor is in it and keyboard keys type into it.
terms.cursor: The blinking line that shows where the next letter will appear.
terms.placeholder: Gray hint text shown when the box is empty.
terms.byte: A small piece of computer memory. Normal letters use 1 byte; emoji use up to 4.
terms.filter: Run text through Roblox's safety check to hide bad words. Required before showing a player's text to other players.
terms.RemoteEvent: A messenger that lets a LocalScript send information to the server.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone.

examples.title: Type a code and press Enter
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

local box = Instance.new("TextBox")
box.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)
box.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5)
box.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(300, 50)
box.PlaceholderText = "Type a code and press Enter"
box.Text = ""
box.TextSize = 22
box.ClearTextOnFocus = false
box.Parent = screenGui

box.FocusLost:Connect(function(enterPressed)
	if not enterPressed then
		return -- they clicked away without pressing Enter
	end
	if string.upper(box.Text) == "FREECOINS" then
		print("Code accepted!")
	else
		print("Unknown code")
	end
	box.Text = ""
end)
explain: We make a centered 300x50 TextBox with gray hint text.
FocusLost fires when the player stops typing. enterPressed is true only if they pressed Enter.
string.upper makes the check ignore capital letters, so 'freecoins' also works.
In a real game, send the code to the server with a RemoteEvent and give rewards there, so players can't cheat.

gotchas: ClearTextOnFocus is true by default, so clicking the box wipes old text. Turn it off if players should edit existing text.
Read box.Text in FocusLost, not on every key press, unless you really need live updates.
Anything a player types that other players will see (signs, pet names, chat) must be filtered with TextService:FilterStringAsync on the server, or your game could be moderated.
Never trust typed text for important stuff on the client. Check it on the server.
UIGradient doesn't work on a TextBox.

class/TextBoxService.s: A service that manages a user's `Class.TextBox` state during gameplay.

class/TextButton.d:
A TextButton behaves similarly to TextLabel in regards to rendering, with the additional behaviors of a GuiButton.

You can disable text rendering by setting TextTransparency to 1. This will result in a plain rectangle that can be used as a button.
class/TextButton.s: A 2D user interface element that displays interactive text.

m.d:
This property provides a copy of Text that contains exactly what is being rendered by the TextButton. This is useful for eliminating style tags used for rich text markup; for example, when RichText is enabled, the ContentText property shows the text as it appears to the user.

RichText Text ContentText
false <b>Hello,<br/> world!</b> <b>Hello,<br/> world!</b>
true <b>Hello,<br/> world!</b> Hello,
world!
m.s: A copy of `Class.TextButton.Text` that contains exactly what is being rendered by the `Class.TextButton`.

kid.simple: Read-only. The text exactly as players see it. If RichText is on, the formatting tags like are removed. For Text = "Hi" with RichText on, ContentText is "Hi".
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
print(button.ContentText)

m.d:
This property selects one of several pre-defined fonts with which the TextButton will render its text. Some fonts have bold, italic and/or light variants.

With the exception of the Font.Legacy font, each font will render text with the line height equal to the TextSize property.

The Font.Code font is the only monospace font. It has the unique property that each character has the exact same width and height ratio of 1:2, where the width of each character is approximately half the TextSize property.

This property is kept in sync with the FontFace property.
m.s: Determines the font used to render text.

kid.simple: Picks a built-in font from a list (Enum.Font), like Gotham or Cartoon. It stays in sync with FontFace; FontFace is the newer, more flexible choice.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.Font = Enum.Font.GothamBold

m.d:
This property is similar to the Font property but allows setting fonts that don't exist in Font.

This property is kept in sync with the Font property, such that when setting FontFace, the font is set to the corresponding Font value or to Font.Unknown if there are no matches.
m.s: Determines the font used to render text.

kid.simple: The font used to draw the text, including its weight (how bold) and style (italic). It can use fonts that aren't in the old Font list.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.FontFace = Font.new("rbxasset://fonts/families/FredokaOne.json")
-- A bold font: pass the weight when you make it
button.FontFace = Font.new("rbxasset://fonts/families/GothamSSm.json", Enum.FontWeight.Bold)

m.d: This property determines the font size to be used.
m.s: Determines the font size to be used.
m.dep: This property is deprecated in favor of TextSize which is an integer and not an enum and thus offers far more options for sizes.

kid.simple: Old — use TextSize instead.

m.d: Controls the height of lines as a multiple of the font's em square size by scaling the spacing between lines of text in the TextButton. Valid values range from 1.0 to 3.0, defaulting to 1.0.
m.s: Scales the spacing between lines of text in the `Class.TextButton`.

kid.simple: The space between lines of text, as a multiplier from 1 to 3. 1 is normal, 1.5 adds extra breathing room, 2 is double spacing.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.LineHeight = 1.5

m.d: This property sets whether a TextButton should regard GuiBase2d.Localize or not.
m.s: Sets whether a `Class.TextButton` should be `Class.GuiBase2d.Localize` or not.

kid.simple: Read-only. The translated text actually being shown, when automatic translation (AutoLocalize) found a translation for the player's language. If no translation applies, it's just the normal text.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
print("Showing:", button.LocalizedText)

m.d:
This property controls the maximum number of graphemes (or units of text) that are shown on the TextButton. It is primarily provided as an easy way to create a typewriter effect where the characters appear one at a time.

Changing the property does not change the position or size of the visible graphemes; the layout will be calculated as if all graphemes are visible.

Setting the property to -1 disables the limit and shows the entirety of the Text.
m.s: The maximum number of graphemes the `Class.TextButton` can show.

kid.simple: Limits how many characters are shown. -1 (default) shows everything. Count up from 0 to make a 'typewriter' effect where letters appear one by one.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.Text = "Welcome, adventurer!"
for i = 0, #button.Text do
	button.MaxVisibleGraphemes = i
	task.wait(0.05)
end
button.MaxVisibleGraphemes = -1 -- show everything
kid.gotcha: The text layout doesn't move while letters appear; it's planned as if all the text is already there.

m.d:
A comma-separated list of OpenType feature tags applied to text rendered by the TextButton (for example, zero for slashed zeros). Whitespace around each tag is ignored. Defaults to an empty string, which applies no additional features.

Only a supported subset of tags is applied. If a tag can't be parsed, isn't supported, or uses unsupported partial enabling with brackets, all tags are discarded. OpenTypeFeaturesError.
m.s: Applies OpenType font features, such as stylistic sets, to the text rendered by the `Class.TextButton`.

kid.simple: Turns on special font features using short codes separated by commas, like "zero" for a zero with a slash through it. Empty (default) means none. If a code doesn't work, OpenTypeFeaturesError says why.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.OpenTypeFeatures = "zero" -- slashed zeros, so 0 doesn't look like O

m.d: Read-only message produced when a tag in OpenTypeFeatures can't be applied — for example, when a tag fails to parse, isn't supported, or uses unsupported partial (bracketed) enabling. Empty while the current OpenTypeFeatures value applies successfully.
m.s: Read-only property that contains the error message, if any, produced while applying `Class.TextButton.OpenTypeFeatures|OpenTypeFeatures`.

kid.simple: Read-only. Empty when OpenTypeFeatures worked. Otherwise a message like "Unsupported feature: xyz" telling you what went wrong.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
if button.OpenTypeFeaturesError ~= "" then
	warn(button.OpenTypeFeaturesError)
end

m.d:
This property determines whether the TextButton renders its text using rich text markup to style sections of the string in bold, italics, specific colors, and more.

To use rich text, simply include rich text formatting tags in the Text string.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.TextButton` renders its text using rich text formatting.

kid.simple: When true, you can style parts of the text with tags like bold, italic or red.
kid.example: local button = script.Parent button.RichText = true button.Text = "You found a golden sword!"

m.d:
This property determines the text content rendered by the TextButton. The visual properties of the string rendered to the screen is determined by TextColor3, TextTransparency, TextSize, Font, TextScaled, TextWrapped, TextXAlignment and TextYAlignment.

It is possible to render emoji such as 🔒 and other symbols which aren't affected by the TextColor3 property. These can be pasted into Script and LocalScript objects, as well as the field within the Properties window.

This property may contain newline characters. Similarly, this property may contain a tab character, but it will render as a space instead.
m.s: Determines the string rendered by the `Class.TextButton`.

kid.simple: The words shown. You can use \n in a script to start a new line.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.Text = "Line one\nLine two"

m.d:
This read-only property reflects the absolute size of rendered text in offsets, meaning that if you try to fit text into a rectangle, this property would reflect the minimum dimensions of the rectangle you'd need in order to fit the text.

Using TextService:GetTextSize(), you can predict what TextBounds will be given a string, Font, TextSize, and frame size.
m.s: Read-only property which reflects the absolute size of rendered text in offsets.

kid.simple: Read-only. The size in pixels of the box the text actually needs. Handy for making a background exactly fit the text.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
print("Text needs", button.TextBounds.X, "by", button.TextBounds.Y, "pixels")

m.d: This property determines the color of text.
m.s: Determines the color of text.

m.s: A boolean representation of whether the button's text fits within the size of it.

local button = script.Parent

m.d:
This property determines whether text is scaled so that it fills the button's entire space. When enabled, TextSize is ignored and TextWrapped is automatically enabled. This property is useful for rendering text elements within BillboardGuis. When this property is used for on-screen UI, it may be helpful to use a UITextSizeConstraint to restrict the range of possible text sizes.

Automatic Sizing

It's recommended that you avoid usage of TextScaled and adjust UI to take advantage of the AutomaticSize property instead. Here are the core differences between the two properties:

  • TextScaled scales the content (text) to accommodate the UI. Without careful consideration, some text may become unreadable if scaled too small.

  • AutomaticSize resizes the UI to accommodate content while maintaining a consistent font size. For more information, see here.

Additionally, it's recommended that you avoid applying both AutomaticSize and TextScaled and to the same TextButton. AutomaticSize determines the maximum amount of available space that a GuiObject can use (in this case, text), while TextScaled uses the available space determined by AutomaticSize to scale the font size up to the maximum font size (100) if there are no size constraints.
m.s: Changes whether text is resized to fit within the `Class.TextButton`.

kid.simple: When true, the text automatically grows or shrinks to fill the whole box (TextSize is ignored and wrapping turns on). Great for BillboardGuis and SurfaceGuis.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.TextScaled = true
kid.gotcha: Text can become tiny and hard to read. Add a UITextSizeConstraint to set a min/max size, and don't combine it with AutomaticSize.

m.d: This property determines the height of one line of rendered text. The unit is in offsets, not points (which is used in most document editing programs). The Font.Legacy font does not hold this property.
m.s: Determines the line height of text in offsets.

kid.simple: How tall one line of text is, in pixels. 14 is small, 24 is medium, 48 is big. Ignored when TextScaled is on.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.TextSize = 24
kid.gotcha: Try not to go below 9; tiny text is hard to read for many players.

m.d:
This property sets the color of the stroke, or outline, of rendered text. Along with TextStrokeTransparency, it determines the final visual appearance of the text stroke.

As a powerful alternative which supports color gradients, see UIStroke.
m.s: Determines the color of the text stroke (outline).

kid.simple: The color of the outline drawn around each letter. Only shows when TextStrokeTransparency is less than 1.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.TextStrokeColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 0) -- black outline
button.TextStrokeTransparency = 0             -- make it visible
kid.gotcha: For thicker or gradient outlines, use a UIStroke instead.

m.d:
This property sets the transparency of the stroke, or outline, of rendered text. Along with TextStrokeColor3, it determines the final visual appearance of the text stroke.

Note that text stroke is multiple renderings of the same transparency, so this property is essentially multiplicative on itself four times over. Therefore, it's recommended to set TextStrokeTransparency to a value in the range of 0.75 to 1 for more a more subtle effect.

As a powerful alternative which supports color gradients, see UIStroke.
m.s: Determines the transparency of the text stroke (outline).

kid.simple: How see-through the letter outline is. 1 (default) = no outline, 0 = solid outline. The outline is drawn several times stacked, so even 0.5 looks quite solid; 0.75 to 1 gives a soft outline.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.TextStrokeTransparency = 0.5

m.d: This property determines the transparency of all the text rendered by the TextButton.
m.s: Determines the transparency of rendered text.

kid.simple: How see-through the text is. 0 = solid, 1 = invisible. Doesn't affect the background box (that's BackgroundTransparency).
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local button = script.Parent
-- Fade the text out over 1 second
TweenService:Create(button, TweenInfo.new(1), {TextTransparency = 1}):Play()

m.d: Controls the truncation of the text displayed in the TextButton.
m.s: Controls the truncation of the text displayed in the `Class.TextButton`.

kid.simple: What to do with text that's too long to fit. None (default) just cuts it off. AtEnd replaces the end with "...". SplitWord can cut in the middle of a word.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.TextTruncate = Enum.TextTruncate.AtEnd -- "A really long na..."

m.d: This property determines whether or not text should wrap at the edges of the TextButton element's space.
m.s: Determines whether or not text should wrap at the edges of the `Class.TextButton` element's space.
m.dep: This item has been superseded by TextButton.TextWrapped which should be used in all new work.

kid.simple: Old — use TextWrapped instead.

m.d:
When enabled, this property will render text on multiple lines within a TextButton element's space so that TextBounds will never exceed the GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize of the element. This is achieved by breaking long lines of text into multiple lines.

Line breaks will prefer whitespace; should a long unbroken word exceed the width of the element, that word will be broken into multiple lines.

If further line breaks would cause the vertical height of the text (the Y component of TextBounds) to exceed the vertical height of the element (the Y component of GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize), then that line will not be rendered at all.
m.s: Determines if text wraps to multiple lines within the `Class.TextButton` element's space, truncating excess text.

kid.simple: When true, long text continues on the next line instead of running off the side. It prefers to break at spaces. Lines that don't fit vertically aren't shown.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.TextWrapped = true

m.d:

Note that this property won't affect the read-only properties TextBounds and TextFits.
