This property controls the positional offset of the tool's weld matrix. It is one of several properties used to position how the player character holds the tool.

Other properties that control how a character holds a tool include Tool.GripUp, Tool.GripRight, and Tool.GripForward. All of these properties are stored in a single CFrame in the Tool.Grip property.
m.s: The positional offset of the tool's weld matrix.

kid.simple: Hidden. The position piece of Grip. Just use Tool.Grip.

m.d:
One of the properties that specifies a tool's orientation in a character's hand. This represents the R00, R10, and R20 values of the grip CFrame rotation matrix.

Other tool properties that control how a character holds a tool include Tool.GripUp, Tool.GripForward, and Tool.GripPos. All of these properties are stored in a single CFrame in the Tool.Grip property.
m.s: Represents the `R00`, `R10`, and `R20` values of the grip `Datatype.CFrame` rotation matrix.

kid.simple: Hidden. One piece of the Grip rotation. Just use Tool.Grip.

m.d:
One of the properties that specifies a tool's orientation in a character's hand. This represents the R01, R11, and R21 values of the grip CFrame rotation matrix.

Other tool properties that control how a character holds a tool include Tool.GripRight, Tool.GripForward, and Tool.GripPos. All of these properties are stored in a single CFrame in the Tool.Grip property.
m.s: Represents the `R01`, `R11`, and `R21` values of the grip `Datatype.CFrame` rotation matrix.

kid.simple: Hidden. One piece of the Grip rotation. Just use Tool.Grip.

m.d:
This property controls whether the Tool can be activated without explicitly executing Tool:Activate() in a script.

When set to true, the tool will only fire Tool.Activated when Tool:Activate() is called. This also suppresses the ContextActionService:BindActivate() function.

When set to false, mouse clicks (when the tool is equipped) will also fire Tool.Activated.
m.s: Controls whether the `Class.Tool` can be activated without executing `Class.Tool:Activate()`.

kid.simple: If true, clicking does NOT activate the tool; only your script calling tool:Activate() does. If false (normal), clicks activate it.
kid.example: tool.ManualActivationOnly = true

m.d:
This property determines whether a Tool functions without a handle.

A tool has a handle when it contains a child part named Handle. Tools with handles typically require the player equipping them to hold an object to use them, for instance weapons. Tools without handles typically don't require the player equipping them to hold anything to use them, for instance "fly" or "summon" tools.

When set to true, the tool will function only with a handle. When set to false, the tool will function even without a handle.
m.s: Determines whether a `Class.Tool` functions without a handle.

kid.simple: If true, the tool only works if it has a part named Handle. Set false for tools you don't hold, like a spell or a 'fly' power.
kid.example: tool.RequiresHandle = false -- a spell with nothing to hold

m.d:
The ToolTip property controls the message that will be displayed when the player's Mouse hovers over the Tool in their Backpack.

Generally, the value of this property should describe the what the tool is or its use. For instance, for a shovel tool, you may choose to set the ToolTip to:

tool.ToolTip = "Shovel"

or

tool.ToolTip = "Use to dig"

or

tool.ToolTip = "Shovel - Use to dig"
m.s: Controls the message displayed when the player's mouse hovers over the tool in their backpack.

kid.simple: The little text that appears when the mouse hovers over the tool in the hotbar.
kid.example: tool.ToolTip = "Shovel - Use to dig"

m.d: This function simulates activation of the Tool. The tool must be equipped for this function to work.
m.s: Simulates activation of the `Class.Tool`.

kid.simple: Uses the tool from a script, as if the player clicked. The tool must be equipped.
kid.example: tool:Activate()

m.d: This function simulates deactivation of the Tool. The tool must be equipped for this function to work.
m.s: Simulates deactivation of the `Class.Tool`.

kid.simple: Acts like the player let go of the click. The tool must be equipped.
kid.example: tool:Deactivate()

m.d:
This event fires when the player clicks while the Tool is equipped. It is not fired if the Ctrl key is pressed during the click.

This event is typically used to perform an action when the player uses the tool, for instance to launch a rocket from a rocket launcher weapon tool.

The below code, when placed in a LocalScript, creates a tool in the local player's Backpack and prints "Tool activated" when the player clicks while the created tool is equipped.
m.s: Fires when the player clicks while the tool is equipped.

kid.simple: Fires when the player clicks (or taps) while holding the tool. Doesn't fire if Ctrl is held during the click.

m.d:
This event fires when the player releases their click while the Tool is equipped and activated. It is typically used to perform an action when the player stops using a tool.

The below code, when placed in a LocalScript, creates a tool in the local player's Backpack and prints "Tool deactivated" when the player releases their click while the tool is equipped and activated.
m.s: Fires when the player releases their click while the tool is equipped and activated.

kid.simple: Fires when the player lets go of the click after activating. Good for charge-up attacks: measure the time between Activated and Deactivated.
kid.example:
local startTime = 0
tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    startTime = os.clock()
end)
tool.Deactivated:Connect(function()
    print("Charged for " .. os.clock() - startTime .. " seconds")
end)

m.d:
This event fires when a player equips the Tool (takes it out of their Backpack).

The opposite of this event, Tool.Unequipped, can be used to determine when the player unequips the tool by putting it in their backpack.

Note that this event does not fire when Tool.RequiresHandle is enabled and no handle is present.
m.s: Fires when the tool is equipped.

p.s: The player's mouse.

kid.simple: Fires when the player takes the tool out and holds it. Gives you the player's Mouse.
kid.gotcha: Won't fire if RequiresHandle is true but there's no Handle.

m.d:
This event fires when a player unequips the Tool (puts it in their Backpack).

The opposite of this event, Tool.Equipped, can be used to determine when the player equips the tool by taking it out of their backpack.

Note that this event does not fire when Tool.RequiresHandle is enabled and no handle is present.
m.s: Fires when the tool is unequipped.

kid.simple: Fires when the player puts the tool away (back in the Backpack).

A Tool is an item a player can hold and use, like a sword, a flashlight or a magic wand. Tools sit in the player's Backpack (the bar at the bottom of the screen) and move into the character's hand when equipped. Scripts inside the tool react when the player clicks.
kid.analogy: A Tool is like an item in a video-game hotbar. It waits in your bag until you pick it, then you hold it in your hand and click to use it.
whenToUse: Make weapons, wands, flashlights, keys or any item a player holds.
Give an item that responds when the player clicks or taps.
Put pickup items around the map that players can grab.
kid.where: Put a Tool in StarterPack to give it to everyone each time they spawn, in a player's StarterGear to give it to just them every spawn, straight into their Backpack for this life only, or in Workspace as a pickup. Keep reward tools in ServerStorage or ReplicatedStorage and clone them. When held, the Tool is moved inside the player's Character model.

terms.equip: Take the tool out of the Backpack and hold it. The tool moves into the character Model.
terms.unequip: Put the tool away. It goes back into the Backpack.
terms.Handle: The part named exactly `Handle` inside a tool. It's where the character's hand grabs it.
terms.activate: Use the tool, usually by clicking, tapping, or pressing the gamepad trigger.
terms.Backpack: The player's inventory folder. Tools in it show as buttons at the bottom of the screen.
terms.StarterPack: A service. Tools in it are copied to every player's Backpack each time they spawn.
terms.CFrame: A position plus a rotation stored together.
terms.RemoteEvent: A messenger object that lets a LocalScript tell the server something (or the server tell a player).
terms.server: The Roblox computer that runs the game for everyone and is trusted.

examples.title: A tool that prints when used
examples.place: LocalScript inside a Tool in StarterPack
explain: Put a Part named Handle inside the Tool so the character can hold it (or turn off RequiresHandle).
Equipped fires when the player picks the tool from their hotbar.
Activated fires when they click or tap while holding it.
Unequipped fires when they put it away or switch tools.

examples.title: A healing potion that works for everyone to see
examples.place: Script inside a Tool in StarterPack
examples.code:
local tool = script.Parent
local HEAL_AMOUNT = 30
local COOLDOWN = 5 -- seconds

tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    -- When equipped, the tool is inside the character model
    local character = tool.Parent
    local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if humanoid and tool.Enabled then
        tool.Enabled = false -- turn off while cooling down
        humanoid.Health = math.min(humanoid.Health + HEAL_AMOUNT, humanoid.MaxHealth)
        task.wait(COOLDOWN)
        tool.Enabled = true
    end
end)
explain: This is a server Script, so the healing is real for everyone, not just on the player's screen.
While held, tool.Parent is the character, so we can find the Humanoid there.
math.min makes sure health never goes over MaxHealth.
Setting Enabled to false stops Activated from firing again until the cooldown ends.

gotchas: A physical tool needs exactly one part named `Handle`, or it won't be held. For tools with nothing to hold, set RequiresHandle to false.
Don't anchor tool parts, or the player will get stuck when holding it.
Weld multi-part tools together, or the pieces fall off.
Tools in the Backpack are lost on death. Use StarterPack or StarterGear to give them back every spawn.
Anything only a LocalScript does (like damage) only happens on that player's screen. Do important things in a server Script, or send a RemoteEvent to the server.

class/Torque.d:
A Torque constraint applies constant torque to an assembly from its center of mass. Alternatively:

  • Because the Torque constraint applies constant torque and angular acceleration, very high speeds may result if no other forces are involved. If you want to maintain a more steady velocity over time, use an AngularVelocity constraint.
  • If you only need initial velocity, set the AssemblyAngularVelocity property directly on the assembly.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Relativity

By default, torque is applied relative to Attachment0. If the parent assembly rotates, the torque will change direction to match the adjusted orientation of the attachment.

If RelativeTo is set to World, torque will be applied in world coordinates, independent of the parent or attachment orientations.

If RelativeTo is set to Attachment1, torque will be applied relative to Attachment1 and, if the attachment rotates, change to match its orientation.
class/Torque.s: Applies constant torque to an assembly from its center of mass.

m.d: The CFrame in which the torque is expressed.
m.s: The `Datatype.CFrame` in which the torque is expressed.

kid.simple: Picks whose directions the Torque vector uses: World (the game's fixed directions), Attachment0 (default; turns with the part), or Attachment1 (follows the other attachment).
kid.example:
local twist = workspace.Top.Torque
twist.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World -- always spin around the real up axis

m.d: The strength and direction of the torque.
m.s: The strength and direction of the torque.

kid.simple: How hard and around which line to twist, as a Vector3. (0, 50, 0) twists around Y; (50, 0, 0) around X. A negative number twists the other way.
kid.example:
local twist = workspace.Top.Torque
twist.Torque = Vector3.new(0, -50, 0) -- spin the opposite direction

kid.simple: Torque is an invisible twister. It keeps twisting a part with the same strength all the time, so the part spins faster and faster. You choose which way it twists with a Vector3: the direction of the vector is the line it spins around.
kid.analogy: Torque is like a friend who keeps flicking a fidget spinner. Every flick adds more spin, so it goes faster and faster unless something slows it down.
whenToUse: Make an object spin up over time
Wheels or propellers that you want to speed up gradually
Twisting an object over when hit
kid.where: Create with Instance.new("Torque") and set Attachment0 to an attachment in the part to spin. It always twists around the part's center of mass. Usually set up from a Script on the server.

terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.angular velocity: How fast something spins, and around which axis, measured in radians per second. 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians per second is one full turn every second.
terms.radians: Another way to measure angles. A full circle is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians, which is 360 degrees. `math.rad(90)` turns 90 degrees into radians.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are rigidly joined (for example by welds) so they move as one solid object. A force on any part moves the whole group.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Pushing exactly through it moves the object without spinning it; pushing off to the side also makes it spin.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.attachment space: Directions measured using an attachment's own arrows. If the part tips over, 'up' for the attachment tips over too.
terms.RelativeTo: Chooses whose arrows the numbers use: World (the game world's fixed directions) or Attachment0/Attachment1 (that attachment's own directions, which turn when the part turns).
terms.spin axis: The imaginary stick something spins around. A Torque of Vector3.new(0, 500, 0) spins around the up-down (Y) line, like a merry-go-round.
terms.constant torque: A twist that never changes strength, so the spin speed keeps growing until friction or something else stops it.

examples.title: Spin a floating part like a top
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = false
part.Parent = workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

-- Hold it up so it does not fall (see VectorForce)
local hover = Instance.new("VectorForce")
hover.Attachment0 = attachment
hover.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
hover.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true
hover.Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity, 0)
hover.Parent = part

-- Twist it around the up (Y) axis
local twist = Instance.new("Torque")
twist.Attachment0 = attachment
twist.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
twist.Torque = Vector3.new(0, 50, 0)
twist.Parent = part

task.wait(2)
twist.Enabled = false -- stop adding spin; it keeps spinning at its current speed
print("Spin speed:", part.AssemblyAngularVelocity.Y, "radians per second")
explain: First we cancel gravity with a VectorForce so the part floats.
Torque (0, 50, 0) in World space means 'twist around the up-down line'.
Each moment, the twist adds more spin, so after 2 seconds it is spinning much faster than after 1.
When we turn the Torque off, nothing slows the floating part, so it keeps the spin it already has.

gotchas: Torque never stops adding spin, so things can end up spinning extremely fast. Use AngularVelocity if you want a steady spin speed.
A part sitting on the ground has friction holding it. Small torques may do nothing; try bigger numbers.
Big or heavy parts need much more torque to spin than small light ones.
With RelativeTo = Attachment0 (the default), the spin axis turns with the part. Use World if you want it to always spin around the true up direction.

class/TorsionSpringConstraint.d:
A TorsionSpringConstraint applies a torque based on a relative angle and a relative angular velocity. Specifically, torsion springs try to bring two axes from two parts together in a compliant way.

Correct orientation of a torsion spring's attachments is important. The constraint will attempt to bring the SecondaryAxis of each attachment into alignment. When building mechanisms like swinging doors, ensure that the secondary axes are perpendicular to the intended axis of rotation.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Damping

The Damping value controls how fast the spring's oscillation dies down. A value of 0 allows the spring to oscillate endlessly, while higher values bring the spring to a rest more quickly.

Stiffness

Stiffness sets the torsional strength of the spring. Higher values create a spring that responds with more force.

Limits

Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the MaxAngle value to restrict the spring's range within a cone; it also exposes the Restitution value which defines the elasticity of the attachments when they reach their limit.
class/TorsionSpringConstraint.s: A rotational spring that opposes the angular motion between two axes.

m.d: This property indicates the number of spring coils for visualization. Default value is 8.
m.s: The number of coils visualized for the constraint.

m.d: The current angle, in degrees, of the torsion spring's limiting cone. The limiting cone is formed at the position of the constraint's Attachment0 around its secondary axis with an angle equal to MaxAngle.
m.s: The current angle, in degrees, of the limiting cone.

m.d: Damping constant for the TorsionSpringConstraint. Multiplied to the velocity of the constraint's Attachments to reduce the spring force applied.
m.s: Damping constant for the `Class.TorsionSpringConstraint`. Multiplied to the velocity of the constraint's `Class.Attachment|Attachments` to reduce the spring force applied.

m.dep: This property is deprecated. Use LimitsEnabled instead.

m.d: This property, when enabled, limits the relative angular motion of the secondary axes of attachments through a cone constraint. The default value is false.
m.s: Limits the relative angular motion of the secondary axes of attachments through a cone constraint.

m.d: This property determines the maximum angle (in degrees) of the torsion spring's limiting cone. The limiting cone is formed at the position of the constraint's Attachment0 around its secondary axis with an angle equal to MaxAngle. Default value is 45 degrees.
m.s: The maximum angle of the constraint's limiting cone.

m.d: This property determines the maximum torque supported by the torsion spring. Defaults to 1000.
m.s: The maximum allowable torque provided by the torsion spring.

m.d: This property indicates the visualization radius of the spring, in studs. Default value is 0.4.
m.s: The visualization radius of the spring.

m.d: This property defines how elastic Attachments connected by a TorsionSpringConstraint are when they reach the end of the range specified by MaxAngle, when LimitEnabled is true. The value defaults to 0 and can be any floating number within the range of 0 and 1.
m.s: The restitution coefficient of the cone constraint.

m.d: In the absence of damping, this property is proportional to the opposing torque of the spring. For instance, higher stiffness results in a larger opposing torque, and smaller stiffness results in a smaller opposing torque. The larger the torque value, the faster the axes are pushed together when the relative angle is positive (or away from each other if the relative angle is negative). The value defaults to 100.
m.s: The torsional stiffness of the spring.

class/TouchTransmitter.d:
An internal object used by networking and replication code to transmit BasePart.Touched and BasePart.TouchEnded events.

The TouchTransmitter object named 'TouchInterest' is created and parented to a BasePart when the BasePart.Touched or BasePart.TouchEnded events are listened (connected) to.

Removing the TouchTransmitter will prevent the touched events from working. The TouchTransmitter object can also be removed exclusively on the client. This will prevent collisions from models the client has network ownership of (such as the player's character) from registering.

Note, in almost all circumstances developers should disconnect the connection using RBXScriptConnection:Disconnect() method rather than removing the TouchTransmitter. Otherwise the connection will not be cleaned up which can cause performance issues over time.
class/TouchTransmitter.s: An internal object used by networking and replication code to transmit `Class.BasePart.Touched` and `Class.BasePart.TouchEnded` events.

class/Trail.d:
The Trail object is used to create a trail effect between two attachments. As the attachments move through space, a texture is drawn on their defined plane. This is commonly used to create effects that visualize movements like tracer trails behind projectiles, footprints, tire tracks, and similar effects.

See Trails for more information.
class/Trail.s: Used to create a trail effect between two attachments.

m.d:
A Trail starts drawing its segments at the positions of its Attachment0 and Attachment1. When the trail is Enabled, it records the positions of its attachments every frame and connects these positions to the attachments' positions on the previous frame, creating a polygon that is then filled in by the trail's Color and Texture.

Changing the attachments of a trail while a trail is drawing will remove all of the segments the trail has already drawn.
m.s: Along with `Class.Trail.Attachment1|Attachment1`, determines where the trail will start drawing its segments.

m.d:
A Trail starts drawing its segments at the positions of its Attachment0 and Attachment1. When the trail is Enabled, it records the positions of its attachments every frame and connects these positions to the attachments' positions on the previous frame, creating a polygon that is then filled in by the trail's Color and Texture.

Changing the attachments of a trail while a trail is drawing will remove all of the segments the trail has already drawn.
m.s: Along with `Class.Trail.Attachment0|Attachment0`, determines where the trail will start drawing its segments.

m.d: Scales the light emitted from the trail when LightInfluence is less than 1. This property is 1 by default and can set to any number within the range of 0 to 10000. Increasing the value of LightInfluence decreases the effect of this property's value.
m.s: Scales the light emitted from the trail when `Class.Trail.LightInfluence|LightInfluence` is less than 1.

m.d:
Determines the color of the trail throughout its lifetime. If Texture is set, this color will tint the texture.

This property is a ColorSequence, allowing the color to be configured to vary across the length of the trail. If the color changes after some of the trail segments have been drawn, all of the old segments will be updated to match the new colors.
m.s: The color of the trail throughout its lifetime.

m.d:
This property determines whether the trail will be drawn or not.

If set to false while a trail is drawing, no new segments will be drawn, but any existing segments will be cleaned up naturally when they reach the end of their Lifetime. To forcibly clean up existing segments, call the Clear() method at the same time.
m.s: Determines whether the trail will be drawn or not.

m.d:
A Trail is a 2D projection existing in 3D space, meaning that it may not be visible from every angle. The FaceCamera property, when set to true, ensures that the trail always faces the CurrentCamera, regardless of its orientation.

Changing this property immediately affects all existing and future trail segments.
m.s: Determines whether the trail will always face the camera, regardless of its orientation.

m.d:
The Lifetime property determines how long each segment in a trail will last, in seconds, before it disappears. Defaults to 2 seconds but can be set anywhere between 0.01 and 20.

The lifetime of a trail is also used by that effect's Color and Transparency properties to determine how each segment is drawn. Both of these properties are sequences, meaning that they define their values at certain keypoints in the segment's lifetime and then interpolate between the values as the segment ages.

If a trail's lifetime changes, existing segments will immediately behave as if they always had the new lifetime, meaning that if they've existed for longer than the new lifetime, they will be removed immediately.
m.s: Determines how long each segment in a trail will last, in seconds.

m.d:
Determines to what degree the colors of the trail are blended with the colors behind it. It should be set in the range of 0 to 1. A value of 0 uses normal blending modes and a value of 1 uses additive blending.

This property should not be confused with LightInfluence which determines how the trail is affected by environmental light.

Changing this property immediately affects all existing and future segments of the trail.

This property does not cause the trail to light the environment.
m.s: Determines to what degree the colors of the trail are blended with the colors behind it.

m.d:
Determines the degree to which the trail is influenced by the environment's lighting, clamped between 0 and 1. When 0, the trail will be unaffected by the environment's lighting. When 1, it will be fully affected by lighting as a BasePart would be.

Changing this property immediately affects all existing and future segments of the trail.

See also LightEmission which specifies to what degree the colors of the trail are blended with the colors behind it.
m.s: Determines the degree to which the trail is influenced by the environment's lighting.

m.d:
The LocalTransparencyModifier property is a multiplier applied to the trail's Transparency that is only visible to the local client. It does not replicate from client to server and is useful for when a trail should not render for a specific client.

Uses the same formula as BasePart.LocalTransparencyModifier:

1 - ((1 - Transparency) × (1 - LocalTransparencyModifier))

A value of 0 (default) has no effect on the trail's transparency. A value of 1 makes the trail completely invisible to the local client regardless of its Transparency value.
m.s: Determines a multiplier for `Class.Trail.Transparency` that is only visible to the local client.

m.d:
This property determines the maximum length of the trail, in studs. Its value defaults to 0, meaning that the trail will not have a maximum length and trail segments will expire in their Lifetime.

This property can be used alongside the MinLength property which determines the minimum length a trail must be before it's drawn.
m.s: Sets the maximum length of the trail.

m.d:
This property determines the minimum length of the trail, in studs. If neither of the trail's attachments have moved at least this value, no new segments will be created and the endpoints of the current segment will be moved to the current position of the attachments.

Note that changing this property will only affect new segments that are drawn; any old segments that have already been drawn will maintain their current length.

This property can be used alongside the MaxLength property which determines the maximum trail length before its oldest segments are erased.
m.s: Sets the minimum length of the trail.

m.d:
The content ID of the texture to be displayed on the trail. If this property is not set, the trail will be displayed as a solid plane; this also occurs when the texture is set to an invalid content ID or the image associated with the texture has not yet loaded.

The appearance of the texture can be further modified by other trail properties including Color and Transparency.

Scaling of the texture is determined by the distance between Attachment0 and Attachment1, as well as the TextureMode, TextureLength, and WidthScale properties.
m.s: The content ID of the texture to be displayed on the trail.

m.d:
The texture displayed on the trail. Supports asset URIs.

This property is the Content equivalent of Texture. Assigning TextureContent updates Texture.

If this property is set to Content.none, the trail displays as a solid plane colored by its Color property. The appearance of the texture can be further modified by Color and Transparency. Scaling of the texture is determined by the distance between Attachment0 and Attachment1, as well as TextureMode, TextureLength, and WidthScale.
m.s: The texture displayed on the trail. Supports [asset URIs](../../../projects/assets/index.md#asset-uris).

m.d: Sets the length of the trail's texture, dependent on TextureMode. Changing this property immediately affects all existing and future trail segments.
m.s: Sets the length of the trail's texture, dependent on `Class.Trail.TextureMode|TextureMode`.

m.d:
This property, alongside TextureLength, determines how a trail's Texture scales, repeats, and moves along with the trail's attachments. Changing this property immediately affects all existing and future trail segments.

Scale and Repetition

When TextureMode is set to TextureMode.Wrap or TextureMode.Static, the TextureLength property sets the length of the texture as it repeats across the trail's length.

When TextureMode is set to TextureMode.Stretch, the texture will repeat TextureLength times across the trail's overall length.

Movement

The TextureMode property also affects the movement of the trail's texture as follows:

  • If set to TextureMode.Stretch, the texture will stretch out based on the lifetime of the trail, and shrink inwards if the trail's attachments stop moving.

  • If set to TextureMode.Wrap, the texture will be tiled as the length of the trail changes, but the textures will remain stationary relative to their attachments.

  • If set to TextureMode.Static, the texture will be rolled out as the attachments move, and they will remain in place until their lifetime is met. This setting is ideal for trail textures that should appear "stamped" where rendered, such as paw prints or tire tracks.
m.s: Determines the manner in which the `Class.Trail.Texture|Texture` scales, repeats, and moves along with the trail's attachments.

m.d: Sets the transparency of the trail's segments over its Lifetime. This value is a NumberSequence, meaning it can be a static value or can change throughout the lifetime of the trail segments.
m.s: Sets the transparency of the trail's segments over its `Class.Trail.Lifetime|Lifetime`.

m.d: This property is a NumberSequence that scales the width of the trail over the course of its lifetime. Values can range between 0 and 1, acting as a multiplier on the distance between the trail's attachments. For example, if the trail's attachments are 2 stud's apart and the value of this property is 0.5, the trail's width will be 1 stud and the trail will be centered between the two attachments.
m.s: Scales the width of the trail over the course of its lifetime.

m.d:
This method immediately clears all segments of the trail and is useful for cleaning up trails with longer lifetimes or for cases where the trail should be removed because of a specific action.

Calling this method only affects existing segments. To clear existing trail segments and temporarily prevent new segments from being drawn, toggle the trail's Enabled property to false at the same time.
m.s: Clears the segments of the trail.

class/Translator.d:
The role of a Translator is to manufacture/return strings localized for the viewing player. It can be used to retrieve display-ready localized text from a LocalizationTable. The source of the Translator.LocaleId property, the set of tables it will search, and the order it will search them in depends on which method was used to create the Translator instance.

The input for a Translator is the original development language string and a context, where all or part of the context can be used to find a more precise/situational translation for the source string.

The Translator can also be used to manufacture translated strings with inserts (data replacements) which may change order based on the target language.
class/Translator.s: The role of a Translator is to manufacture/return strings localized for the viewing player.

m.d: The Roblox locale of the output translated strings from this table, for example "en-us" or "es-es." Defaults to "en-us".
m.s: The locale of translated strings.

m.d:
Returns the localized text string in a LocalizationTable based on its Translator locale, by key. The optional args table is used for filling format parameters in the matching text entry.

Note that this method will throw an error in the following cases:

  • If none of the LocalizationTables available to this Translator include a value for the given key.
  • If the format string for the key uses numbered parameters and args is not an array.
  • If the format string uses named parameters and args is not a table of key-value pairs.
  • If args is missing values for parameters that are used in the matching format string.

See Localize with scripting for more details and usage examples of this function.
m.s: Returns the localized text string in a `Class.LocalizationTable` based on its `Class.Translator` locale, by key.

p.s: The Key value to look up and translate.
To be provided if the Source text and translations contain format strings. Will be a Luau table of values or key-value pairs, depending on whether the format strings are numbered or named.

r.s: The localized text string associated with the given key, with any format parameters filled in from args.

m.d:
Returns the localized text string in a LocalizationTable based on its Translator locale. This string will be in the context of the provided object, given the provided Source text.

See Localize with scripting for more details and usage examples of this function.

Context Overrides

In some cases, duplicate Source strings may have completely different translations in other languages. For example, the English noun "Screen" can indicate both a computer screen and a window screen, but the Spanish translations are completely different:

A B C D E
Key Context Source Example es
Screen Pantalla
Screen Mosquitero

In these cases, the first argument to this function — a valid in-game Instance — can be used as a "tie breaker" when multiple GUI objects use the same source string. To implement this, specify the "path" to the Instance you'd like to override as the Context value of the translation data:

A B C D E
Key Context Source Example es
workspace.ComputerScreen.SurfaceGui.TextLabel Screen Pantalla
Screen Mosquitero

Then, when calling this function in a script, pass the same Instance as the first argument, followed by the Source lookup text as the second argument:
m.s: Returns the localized text string in a `Class.LocalizationTable` based on its `Class.Translator` locale, by source lookup.

p.s: A valid in-game Instance to use for context override as outlined above. Note that this argument can be arbitrary, for example game, if you don't require a context override.
The Source text to look up and translate.

class/TremoloSoundEffect.d:
The TremoloSoundEffect creates a trembling effect on a sound by varying the volume of the sound up and down.

Like all other SoundEffects, a TremoloSoundEffect can be applied either to a Sound or SoundGroup by being parented to either.
class/TremoloSoundEffect.s: Creates a trembling effect on a sound by varying the volume of the sound up and down.

m.d: Range: 0 to 1 (default 1) Controls how much the volume will raise and lower. This value ranges between 0 (minimum volume) and 1 (maximum volume). If set to its minimum, the volume will not oscillate at all.
m.s: Controls how much the volume will raise and lower.

m.d: Range: 0 to 1 (default 0.5) Controls how long during one volume oscillation the effect will be active, specifically what percentage between 0 (0%) and 1 (100%).
m.s: Controls how long during one volume oscillation the effect will be active.

m.d: Range: 0.1 to 20 (default 5) Sets how often the effect will oscillate the volume. Measured in Hz.
m.s: Sets how often the effect will oscillate the volume.

class/TriangleMeshPart.d: TriangleMeshPart is an abstract intermediate class from which MeshPart and PartOperation inherit. It was created to consolidate the management of physical geometry properties between the two sub-classes. It implements the read-only CollisionFidelity and CollisionPrecision.
class/TriangleMeshPart.s: Abstract intermediate class that manages physical geometry properties for PartOperations and MeshParts.

m.d:
This property determines how the collision model of the TriangleMeshPart relates to the actual geometry of the mesh. This property cannot be read or manipulated by scripts during runtime.

See here for a visual representation of the various options.
m.s: Determines the level of detail the part's physics will adhere to its mesh.

m.d: This property describes the precision-to-performance tradeoff of the part's collision geometry when TriangleMeshPart.CollisionFidelity is set to CollisionFidelity.Tunable. A value of 0 favors maximum performance with the simplest collision mesh, while a value of 1 favors maximum precision with a collision mesh that closely matches the visual mesh.
m.s: Quantifies how precise or performant a `Enum.CollisionFidelity.Tunable` collision geometry is, from `0` to `1`.

m.d:
Controls which geometric representation the physics engine uses when it computes aerodynamic (fluid) forces and torques for the part. It defaults to FluidFidelity.Automatic, in which the engine selects a representation on your behalf.

  • FluidFidelity.Automatic — the engine chooses the representation; it currently evaluates fluid forces against the part's collision geometry.
  • FluidFidelity.UseCollisionGeometry — fluid forces are evaluated against the part's collision geometry, matching the shape used for collision detection.
  • FluidFidelity.UsePreciseGeometry — fluid forces are evaluated against the part's precise mesh geometry, producing more accurate forces at a higher computational cost.

Because this property has plugin-level write security, it is configured in Studio rather than assigned by runtime scripts.

This setting only affects a part while fluid forces are active for the place, which is governed by Workspace.FluidForces (an FluidForces value that defaults to Default; setting it to Experimental enables the aerodynamic force model). When fluid forces are not applied to the part, the chosen fidelity has no effect.
m.s: Determines the geometric representation used to compute aerodynamic forces and torques.

m.d: This read-only property reports the size of the part's mesh geometry when it was loaded, as width, height, and depth in studs. It is not affected by resizing the part through BasePart.Size, so dividing BasePart.Size by MeshSize gives the scale factor currently applied to the mesh's visual and physical geometry.
m.s: The original size of the part's source mesh geometry, before any scaling applied through `Class.BasePart.Size`.

class/TrussPart.d:
A TrussPart is similar to a Part but with a different visual Style and the important distinction that default characters are able to climb it.

This part type has significantly more restrictive size limitations than other parts; it must be 2*2*n studs where n is a multiple of 2 with a maximum of 512.

Additionally, this part type does not support styling through the addition of Decals or Textures. If you wish to create a textured and "climbable" BasePart but also utilize the climbing behavior of TrussPart, consider setting the Transparency of the TrussPart to 1 to make it invisible, set CanCollide on the BasePart to false, and then align the climbable surface of the mesh/model with that of the TrussPart.
class/TrussPart.s: Similar to a `Class.Part` but with a different visual `Class.TrussPart.Style|Style` and the important distinction that default characters are able to climb it.

m.d:
Sets what the truss looks like, from the following options:

  • Style.AlternatingSupports
  • Style.BridgeStyleSupports
  • Style.NoSupports
m.s: Sets what the truss looks like.

class/Tween.d:
The Tween object controls the playback of an interpolation. Creating and configuring a Tween is done with the TweenService:Create() function; Instance.new() cannot be used for this particular object.

Note that while the configuration of a tween can be accessed after a tween has been created, it can not be modified. If new goals are needed for an interpolation, a new Tween must be created.

Also note that multiple tweens can be played on the same object at the same time, but they must not be interpolating the same property. If two tweens attempt to modify the same property, the initial tween will be cancelled and overwritten by the most recent tween.
class/Tween.s: The `Class.Tween` object controls the playback of an interpolation.

m.d: This property of a Tween (read-only) points to the Instance whose properties are being interpolated.
m.s: Read-only property that points to the `Class.Instance` whose properties are being interpolated by the tween.

kid.simple: The object this tween is changing, like the Part or Frame you passed to `TweenService:Create()`. Read-only.
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local tween = TweenService:Create(workspace.Part, TweenInfo.new(1), {Transparency = 1})
print(tween.Instance.Name) -- Part

m.d: Read-only property that includes information on how the interpolation of the Tween is to be carried out, using the TweenInfo data type.
m.s: Read-only property that includes information on how the interpolation of the `Class.Tween` is to be carried out.

kid.simple: The TweenInfo settings this tween was made with: its time, easing style, easing direction, repeat count, reverses and delay. Read-only.
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local tween = TweenService:Create(workspace.Part, TweenInfo.new(3), {Transparency = 1})
print(tween.TweenInfo.Time) -- 3 (seconds)
print(tween.TweenInfo.EasingStyle) -- Enum.EasingStyle.Quad (the default)

kid.simple: A Tween is one ready-to-play smooth animation of an object's properties. You get one from `TweenService:Create()`, then you can Play, Pause or Cancel it, and listen for when it is Completed. Once made, its settings cannot be changed; make a new Tween if you need different goals.
kid.analogy: A Tween is like a recorded TV show. TweenService records it, and the Tween is the remote control: play, pause, stop, and a light that tells you when the show is over.
whenToUse: Start a smooth change with `:Play()`
Pause a moving platform with `:Pause()` and resume it later with `:Play()`
Stop an animation with `:Cancel()`
Do something after an animation ends using `Completed`
kid.where: Server and client. You cannot use `Instance.new("Tween")`; you must make it with `game:GetService("TweenService"):Create(...)`.

terms.tween: Short for "in-between". A smooth change of a property from its current value to a goal value over time.
terms.read-only: You can look at the value, but you cannot change it.
terms.PlaybackState: Where the tween is in its life: `Begin` (made but never played), `Delayed` (waiting for its delay time), `Playing`, `Paused`, `Completed` (finished normally) or `Cancelled` (stopped early).
terms.event: Something that happens in the game that your code can listen for, like a doorbell. You `:Connect` a function to run when it rings.
terms.inherits: Gets features from a parent class. Tween gets Play, Pause, Cancel, PlaybackState and Completed from a class called TweenBase.
terms.TweenInfo: The settings that say how a tween moves: time, easing style, easing direction, repeat count, reverses, and delay.

examples.title: Play, pause and resume a moving platform
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

local platform = script.Parent
platform.Anchored = true

local info = TweenInfo.new(4, Enum.EasingStyle.Linear)
local tween = TweenService:Create(platform, info, {
    Position = platform.Position + Vector3.new(30, 0, 0),
})

tween:Play()
task.wait(2)        -- let it move for 2 seconds (about halfway)
tween:Pause()       -- freeze where it is
print(tween.PlaybackState) -- Enum.PlaybackState.Paused
task.wait(3)
tween:Play()        -- carries on from where it stopped

tween.Completed:Connect(function(state)
    print("Tween ended with state:", state) -- Enum.PlaybackState.Completed
end)
explain: We make a 4-second tween that slides the platform 30 studs along X.
After 2 seconds we pause it. Pausing keeps its progress.
Calling `Play` again continues from where it paused.
`Completed` tells us when it is finished and why (Completed or Cancelled).

gotchas: `Pause` keeps the progress; `Cancel` throws the progress away. After a Cancel, `Play` starts over and takes the full time again.
`Cancel` does NOT put the part back to where it started. It just stops it where it is.
`Pause` does not fire the `Completed` event, but `Cancel` does.
Calling `Play` on a tween that is already playing does nothing.
You cannot change a tween's goal or time after making it. Create a new tween instead.

class/TweenBase.d: Abstract base class for in-between interpolation handlers; parent class of Tween.
class/TweenBase.s: Abstract base class for in-between interpolation handlers. `Class.Tween` inherits from `Class.TweenBase`.

m.d: Read-only property that shows the current stage for the Tween animation. See PlaybackState for descriptions of each state. Change using functions like Tween:Play().
m.s: Read-only property that shows the current state for the `Class.Tween` animation.

kid.simple: Tells you what the tween is doing right now: Begin, Delayed, Playing, Paused, Completed or Cancelled. Read-only; change it by calling Play, Pause or Cancel.
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local tween = TweenService:Create(workspace.Part, TweenInfo.new(2), {Transparency = 1})
print(tween.PlaybackState) -- Enum.PlaybackState.Begin
tween:Play()
print(tween.PlaybackState) -- Enum.PlaybackState.Playing

m.d:
Halts playback of a Tween and resets the tween variables.

Only resets the tween variables, not the properties being changed by the tween. If you cancel a tween halfway through its animation, the properties do not reset to their original values. Differs from TweenBase:Pause() in that once resumed, it takes the full duration of the tween to complete the animation.
m.s: Halts playback and resets the tween variables. If you then call `Class.TweenBase:Play()`, the properties of the tween resume interpolating towards their destination, but take the full length of the animation to do so.

kid.simple: Stops the tween and forgets its progress. The object stays where it was when you cancelled; it does not jump back. If you `Play` again later, it takes the full time to reach the goal. Fires `Completed` with the state Cancelled.
kid.example:
tween:Play()
task.wait(1)
tween:Cancel() -- stop now; the part stays wherever it got to
kid.gotcha: Cancel does not undo the changes. If you want the part back at the start, set its property back yourself or tween it back.

m.d:
Halts playback of the tween. Doesn't reset its progress variables, meaning that if you call TweenBase:Play(), the tween resumes playback from the moment it was paused.

If you want to reset the progress variables of the tween, use TweenBase:Cancel().

You can only pause tweens that are in the PlaybackState of PlaybackState.Playing; tweens in other states won't pause. If a tween is in a different PlaybackState such as PlaybackState.Delayed (as a result of its TweenInfo.DelayTime being greater than 0), attempting to pause the tween will fail and the tween will play following its specified delay time.
m.s: Halts playback of the tween. Doesn't reset its progress variables, meaning that if you call `Class.TweenBase:Play()`, the tween resumes playback from the moment it was paused.

kid.simple: Freezes the tween where it is and remembers its progress, so `Play` continues from that spot. Does not fire `Completed`.
kid.example:
tween:Play()
task.wait(0.5)
tween:Pause() -- freeze halfway
task.wait(2)
tween:Play()  -- continue from halfway
kid.gotcha: Only a tween that is currently playing can be paused.

m.d:
Starts playback of a tween. Note that if playback has already started, calling Play() has no effect unless the tween has finished or is stopped (either by TweenBase:Cancel() or TweenBase:Pause()).

Multiple tweens can be played on the same object at the same time, but they must not animate the same property. If two tweens attempt to modify the same property, the initial tween is cancelled and overwritten by the most recent tween (see examples).
m.s: Starts playback of a tween. Note that if playback has already started, calling `Play()` has no effect unless the tween has finished or is stopped (either by `Class.TweenBase:Cancel()` or `Class.TweenBase:Pause()`).

kid.simple: Starts the tween, or continues it after a Pause. If it is already playing, nothing happens.
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local tween = TweenService:Create(workspace.Part, TweenInfo.new(1), {Transparency = 1})
tween:Play() -- the part fades out over 1 second

m.d:
Fires when the tween finishes playing or when stopped with TweenBase:Cancel().

Passes the PlaybackState of the tween to any connected functions to give an indication of why the tween ended. Note that calling TweenBase:Pause() does not fire the Completed event.
m.s: Fires when the tween finishes playing or when stopped with `Class.TweenBase:Cancel()`.

p.s: The PlaybackState of the tween upon completion.

kid.simple: An event that fires when the tween finishes, or when it is cancelled. It tells you which one happened by giving you a PlaybackState (Completed or Cancelled). Pausing does not fire it.
kid.example:
tween.Completed:Connect(function(playbackState)
    if playbackState == Enum.PlaybackState.Completed then
        print("Finished all the way!")
    end
end)
tween:Play()

class/TweenService.d:
TweenService is used to create Tweens which interpolate, or tween, the properties of instances. Tweens can be used on any object with compatible property types, including:

  • number
  • boolean
  • CFrame
  • Rect
  • Color3
  • UDim
  • UDim2
  • Vector2
  • Vector2int16
  • Vector3
  • EnumItem

TweenService:Create(), the primary constructor function, takes TweenInfo specifications about the tween and generates the Tween object which can then be used to play the tween.

Note that Tweens can interpolate multiple properties at the same time, but they must not be interpolating the same property. If two tweens attempt to modify the same property, the initial tween will be cancelled and overwritten by the most recent tween.
class/TweenService.s: Used to create `Class.Tween|Tweens` which interpolate, or tween, the properties of instances.

m.d:
This constructor creates a new Tween from three arguments: the object to tween, the TweenInfo specifications, and a table containing the properties to tween and values to tween to.

The propertyTable parameter needs to be a dictionary where the keys are the string names of the property (for example Position, Transparency, or Color), and the values are the property targets at the end of the tween.

The Tween created using this function is unique to the object given as the instance parameter. To apply the same tween to another object, call this function again with the new object.
m.s: Creates a new `Class.Tween` given the object whose properties are to be tweened, a `Datatype.TweenInfo`, and a dictionary of goal property values.

p.s: The Instance whose properties are to be tweened.
The TweenInfo to be used.
A dictionary of properties, and their target values, to be tweened.

r.s: The newly created Tween configured to interpolate the given properties toward their target values. Call TweenBase:Play() on the returned object to start the tween.

kid.simple: Makes a new Tween. You give it three things: the object to change, a TweenInfo (how long and what easing), and a goal table (which properties and their end values). It returns the Tween, which you start with `:Play()`.
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local part = workspace.Part -- a part named Part in Workspace

local info = TweenInfo.new(1) -- 1 second, default easing (Quad, Out)
local tween = TweenService:Create(part, info, {Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)})
tween:Play() -- the part fades to red over 1 second
kid.gotcha: Each tween works on just one object. To tween 5 parts, call `Create` 5 times (once for each part).

m.d: Returns a new alpha value for interpolating using the given alpha value, EasingStyle, and EasingDirection. The provided alpha value will be clamped between 0 and 1. This method raises an error if easingStyle is EasingStyle.Bezier or EasingStyle.Spring.
m.s: Calculates a new alpha given an `Enum.EasingStyle` and `Enum.EasingDirection`.

p.s: An interpolation value between 0 and 1.
The easing style to use.
The easing direction to use.

r.s: A new alpha value generated from the given easing style and direction.

kid.simple: A math helper that turns a plain progress number (alpha, from 0 to 1) into an eased progress number, using an easing style and direction. Use it when you want to move something yourself (for example inside a loop) but still want that smooth tween feel.
kid.example:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

-- alpha 0.5 means halfway through the time
local eased = TweenService:GetValue(0.5, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.In)
print(eased) -- 0.25: with Quad In, halfway through the time you are only 25% of the way there

local linear = TweenService:GetValue(0.5, Enum.EasingStyle.Linear, Enum.EasingDirection.In)
print(linear) -- 0.5: Linear keeps a steady speed
kid.gotcha: Alpha numbers smaller than 0 or bigger than 1 get squeezed back into the 0 to 1 range. `Bezier` and `Spring` styles cause an error here.

m.d: Smoothly interpolates a value towards a target, simulating a critically damped spring. Returns a tuple with (newValue, newVelocity). newVelocity needs to be fed to the next call of SmoothDamp to ensure smooth results. Supports number, Vector2, Vector3, and CFrame.
m.s: Smoothly interpolates a value towards a target, simulating a critically damped spring.

p.s: The current value to smooth.
The target value to reach.

The current velocity with which the current value should approach the target value. You shouldn't modify this value between calls yourself, it's used to store the stateful velocity. In most cases, initialize this with 0, Vector2.zero, Vector3.zero, or CFrame.identity depending on the type, or if needed, with your initial velocity.

The duration over which the total smoothing operation should take place. Note that since this is a damped spring, there's no guarantee current will be exactly target after this time, but it will be close. Smaller values result in quicker smoothing.
The maximum speed at which the current value should approach the target value. Leaving this nil defaults to math.huge, meaning the velocity isn't clamped.
The rate at which the smoothing operation should be applied. If left nil, the current engine delta time will be used.

r.s: The new value and new velocity calculated from the smoothing operation.

kid.simple: Moves a value a little bit toward a target each time you call it, like a soft spring that slows down as it arrives without bouncing. It returns two things: the new value and the new velocity (speed). Give that velocity back to the next call so the motion stays smooth. Works with numbers, Vector2, Vector3 and CFrame. Great for a part or camera that smoothly follows something.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts: a part smoothly follows a target part
local RunService = game:GetService("RunService")
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

local follower = workspace:WaitForChild("Follower")
local target = workspace:WaitForChild("Target")
follower.Anchored = true

local velocity = Vector3.zero -- start with no speed

RunService.PreRender:Connect(function(deltaTime)
    -- smoothTime 0.3: reach the target in about 0.3 seconds
    local newPos
    newPos, velocity = TweenService:SmoothDamp(follower.Position, target.Position, velocity, 0.3, nil, deltaTime)
    follower.Position = newPos
end)
kid.gotcha: Always save the returned velocity and pass it into the next call. If you reset it to zero every frame, the motion will be jerky.

kid.simple: TweenService makes things change smoothly over time instead of all at once. You tell it what object to change, what the property should end up as, and how long it should take. It then slides the value there for you, frame by frame. It is great for doors that slide open, buttons that grow, or colors that fade.
kid.analogy: TweenService is like a flip-book artist. You draw the first page and the last page, and it draws all the pages in between so the movement looks smooth.
whenToUse: Slide a door, platform or elevator from one spot to another
Fade a part or a GUI in or out by changing `Transparency`
Smoothly change a color, size or rotation
Make menu buttons grow or bounce when hovered
Get a nice smooth curve number with `GetValue` for your own animations
kid.where: Server and client. Get it with game:GetService("TweenService"). Tweens made on the server are seen by everyone; tweens made in a LocalScript are only seen by that one player (and look smoother for them).

terms.tween: Short for "in-between". The game smoothly fills in all the in-between steps so a change looks like a slide instead of a jump.
terms.interpolate: To fill in the values between a start and an end. Going from 0 to 10 in 1 second, halfway through you are at 5.
terms.property: A setting on an object, like a part's `Position`, `Color`, `Size` or `Transparency`.
terms.TweenInfo: A small settings package that says HOW the tween moves: how long it takes, which easing style and direction, how many times it repeats, whether it plays backwards, and how long to wait before starting.
terms.easing style: The shape of the speed change during the tween. `Linear` keeps the same speed the whole time. `Quad`, `Cubic`, `Quart`, `Quint` and `Exponential` speed up or slow down, each one more sharply than the last. `Sine` is extra gentle. `Back` goes a little too far then comes back. `Bounce` bounces like a dropped ball. `Elastic` wobbles like a rubber band.
terms.easing direction: Which end of the tween gets the easing. `In` = starts slow, ends fast (like a car pulling away). `Out` = starts fast, ends slow (like a car braking to park). `InOut` = slow at both the start and the end, fast in the middle. The default is `Out`.
terms.alpha: A number from 0 to 1 that means "how far along". 0 is the start, 0.5 is halfway, 1 is the end.
terms.instance: Any object in your game, like a Part, a Sound, or a GUI button.
terms.client: The player's own computer or phone. LocalScripts run here.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone. Scripts in ServerScriptService run here.
terms.goal table: The table you give to `Create` that lists each property name and the value it should end at, like `{Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0), Transparency = 0.5}`.
terms.velocity: How fast something is moving and in which direction.
terms.tuple: When a function hands back more than one value at once, like `local a, b = myFunction()`.
terms.delta time (dt): How many seconds passed since the last frame, usually a tiny number like 0.016 (one sixtieth of a second).

examples.title: Slide a part up and make it see-through
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

local part = script.Parent
part.Anchored = true -- anchored so gravity does not fight the tween

-- HOW to move: 2 seconds, Quad easing, slow down at the end (Out)
local info = TweenInfo.new(2, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)

-- WHAT to change: end 10 studs higher and half see-through
local goal = {
    Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(0, 10, 0),
    Transparency = 0.5,
}

local tween = TweenService:Create(part, info, goal)
tween:Play()

tween.Completed:Wait() -- pause this script until the tween finishes
print("Done moving!")
explain: We get TweenService and the part this script is inside.
`TweenInfo.new(2, ...)` says: take 2 seconds, use the Quad easing style, with the Out direction (start fast, gently slow down at the end).
The goal table lists the END values. If the part starts at (0, 5, 0) it will end at (0, 15, 0), because we added (0, 10, 0).
`Create` builds the tween but does not start it. `Play` starts it.
`tween.Completed:Wait()` waits until it is finished, then we print.

examples.title: A door that opens and closes forever
examples.place: Script inside a Part named Door (in Workspace)
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

local door = script.Parent
door.Anchored = true

-- 1.5 seconds, Sine easing, InOut (gentle start AND gentle stop)
-- repeatCount -1 = repeat forever, reverses true = play backwards too
-- delayTime 1 = wait 1 second before each run
local info = TweenInfo.new(1.5, Enum.EasingStyle.Sine, Enum.EasingDirection.InOut, -1, true, 1)

local tween = TweenService:Create(door, info, {
    CFrame = door.CFrame * CFrame.new(5, 0, 0), -- 5 studs to the door's right
})
tween:Play()
explain: `TweenInfo.new` has 6 settings in order: time, easing style, easing direction, repeat count, reverses, delay time.
A repeat count of -1 means it never stops repeating.
Reverses = true means after sliding open, it slides back closed.
`door.CFrame * CFrame.new(5, 0, 0)` means 5 studs to the right from the door's own point of view (its own right side), not the world's.

examples.title: Try every easing style side by side
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")

local styles = {
    Enum.EasingStyle.Linear, Enum.EasingStyle.Sine, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad,
    Enum.EasingStyle.Cubic, Enum.EasingStyle.Quart, Enum.EasingStyle.Quint,
    Enum.EasingStyle.Exponential, Enum.EasingStyle.Circular,
    Enum.EasingStyle.Back, Enum.EasingStyle.Bounce, Enum.EasingStyle.Elastic,
}

for i, style in styles do
    -- make one part per style, lined up in a row
    local part = Instance.new("Part")
    part.Anchored = true
    part.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
    part.Position = Vector3.new(i * 4, 5, 0)
    part.Name = style.Name
    part.Parent = workspace

    -- all parts move 20 studs forward in 3 seconds, but with different styles
    local info = TweenInfo.new(3, style, Enum.EasingDirection.Out, -1, true)
    TweenService:Create(part, info, {Position = part.Position + Vector3.new(0, 0, 20)}):Play()
end
explain: We make 11 parts in a row, one for each easing style.
They all travel the same distance in the same time, so you can SEE the difference in how they speed up and slow down.
Change `Enum.EasingDirection.Out` to `In` or `InOut` and play again to see what direction does.

gotchas: `TweenService:Create` does not start the tween. You must call `:Play()` on it.
Unanchored parts fall because of gravity while the tween moves them. Set `Anchored = true` on parts you tween.
If two tweens change the SAME property of the same object at once, the newer one wins and the older one is cancelled.
The goal table uses property names as text keys, like `{Transparency = 1}`. A misspelled name (`Transparancy`) causes an error.
Tweening a model: tween the PrimaryPart's CFrame only moves that one part unless the other parts are welded to it.
Only some value types can be tweened: numbers, booleans, CFrame, Rect, Color3, UDim, UDim2, Vector2, Vector2int16, Vector3 and EnumItem. Text (strings) cannot be tweened.
Easing styles `Bezier` and `Spring` cannot be used with `TweenInfo.new` or `GetValue`; they cause an error.
